Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Course purpose and preparation; fingerprint d865f97f1915a5acc993b0e7765ad1e7018c7c12b7aacc5ec2b44cc6c1b2af21. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Course purpose and preparation

This is the second undergraduate econometrics course. Its purpose is to enable independent empirical work: translate a research question into a regression equation, select a data structure and method, estimate it in statistical software, assess the assumptions, and interpret the results. The lecture emphasizes understanding the data-generating process because economic data do not automatically meet the assumptions of an exact statistical model. The SIS export lists 6 ECTS, Econometrics I (JEB109) as a prerequisite, and JEB125 as a course for which this course is a prerequisite. Lecture 1, PDF pp. 10–12; SIS export, PDF p. 1

The lecturer is Barbara Pertold-Gebicka; the seminar leaders are Veronika Plachá, Oliver Škultéty, and Kai Wang. The uploaded schedule gives Wednesday lectures at 12:30–13:50 and seminars on Wednesday at 15:30–16:50 or 18:30–19:50, or Thursday at 14:00–15:20. The lecture lists room 016 for seminars. Prepare by reading the assigned material and revising prerequisite methods before the lecture or seminar. Week 1's lecture is September 30, and the seminar handout is dated September 30 / October 1, 2026. Lecture 1, PDF pp. 2, 5, 12; Syllabus 2026, PDF pp. 1–2; Seminar 1, PDF p. 1, header

The main textbook is Jeffrey M. Wooldridge's Introductory Econometrics: A Modern Approach, fourth edition or higher according to the lecture. The lecture recommends Chris Brooks, Angrist and Pischke, and Cameron and Trivedi as complementary readings; the SIS export lists Brooks and Cameron and Trivedi. These are reading references, not sources ingested in this pass. R is the official seminar software. The lecture permits other software in home assignments, while the syllabus and SIS export request appended R code; students should clarify expectations if using another package. Lecture 1, PDF pp. 4, 7; Syllabus 2026, PDF p. 1; SIS export, PDF p. 2

Assessment and submitted work

Four assignments are worth up to 10 points each (40 total), the midterm up to 20, and the final up to 40. Passing requires more than 20 final-exam points; the lecture expresses this as at least 21 points and more than 50% of the final. A good overall total cannot replace this separate final-exam requirement. The midterm is one-shot; the lecture gives November 11, 2026, at 12:30. The final takes place in the exam period, and the lecture permits three trials. Lecture 1, PDF pp. 6, 9; Syllabus 2026, PDF p. 2

Assignments combine a theoretical problem and an empirical problem treated as a small project with a short report. Lecture 1 says “Work in groups of 2 students,” whereas the syllabus and SIS export encourage groups of two; the source wording differs in whether pairing is expressed as a requirement or encouragement. The syllabus says each such group submits one solution naming both participants, appends R code, and meets the stated deadline because late work receives no credit. The lecture promises assignment feedback within 10 working days and exam scores within 7 working days. Lecture 1, PDF pp. 7–9; Syllabus 2026, PDF p. 1

The midterm uses multiple-choice and YES/NO questions according to Lecture 1. Its stated scope is the first six lectures, testing theoretical and practical knowledge. The final covers the whole course and includes true/false, open theoretical, and open practical questions. The SIS export explicitly describes both exams as compulsory and in person. These statements record the supplied exam formats and scope; they do not ingest the later lecture content. Lecture 1, PDF p. 9; Syllabus 2026, PDF p. 2; SIS export, PDF p. 2

sections.html:
Self-assessment criteria and tutor checks

Pass: all C1–C4 correct, essential reasoning explicit, known independent conditions and fresh item. Partial: one or more components missing, an unexplained claim, or a recoverable arithmetic slip with sound method. Fail: a critical conceptual error, wrong method/assumptions/interpretation, or no usable attempt. Unscorable: unknown conditions/exposure or an alternative outside the prepared key. Equivalent algebra, clear verbal reasoning and synonymous units/assumption names are acceptable; assumption numbers alone are insufficient. Numerical rounding to sensible precision is acceptable. A isolated arithmetic slip is partial and is not treated as established conceptual failure; the learner must independently repair it with a fresh prepared full item before a pass qualifies. No numeric grading scale is invented.

Every full task I1, I2, D1, D2 expressly requests all C1–C4 and has a complete task-specific key plus exact conceptual reasoning above. Omitted pieces are partial even if an unasked answer happens to sound fluent. Supported S and narrow correction C never substitute for a full check.

Permitted acquisition routes: I1+I2; if an item was exposed, failed or unavailable, replace only that full check with a previously unexposed D1 or D2. Any selected pair of distinct items from {I1,I2,D1,D2} covers C1–C4 twice. Do not use an item twice or count a corrected answer to the same item as fresh. D items used immediately are logged as independent replacement checks, not delayed evidence. No shortened variant or arbitrary new task is permitted. Two complete unassisted passes under O001-C2 establish acquisition; they do not establish retention. This is a default evidence rule, not a learner outcome.

Sign: choosing the most convenient date, inventing a fractional rounding rule, or saying a high total overrides final 20. Treat as tentative after one omission; a stated rule is a critical error. Correction: source disagreement is information, not permission to choose; apply the final gate separately from total. Hint1: separate total from final condition. Hint2: compare20 with “more than 20”.

Score the original response before help. One ambiguous error only suggests a tentative misconception; establish it only from explicit reasoning or repeated diagnostic signs. Explain the relevant prepared step and its consequence; never label the learner from confidence or a single slip.

sections.html:
Derive the OLS normal equations and centered solution, calculate fitted values/residuals, use matrix dimensions/full rank, and distinguish algebraic fitting identities from population assumptions. The question is what the available information lets us calculate or conclude, and which extra conditions the conclusion needs.

Population model \(y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1 x_i+u_i\): fixed population parameters, generally unobserved disturbance. Hats mark sample estimates; \(\hat u_i=y_i-\hat y_i\) is an observable fitted residual. Slope units are \(y\) units per \(x\) unit; intercept at \(x=0\) needs substantive relevance. \(S_{xx}=\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2\), \(S_{xy}=\sum(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)\). In multiple regression \(X\) includes ones; \(k\) counts nonconstant regressors. OLS can be calculated without certifying a causal relationship.
sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
1. Minimize \(Q(b)=\sum(y_i-b_0-b_1 x_i)^2\). Derivatives are \(-2\sum\hat u_i\) and \(-2\sum x_i\hat u_i\); set both to zero.
  2. The first implies \(b_0=\bar y-b_1\bar x\). Substitute into the second: \(S_{xy}-b_1 S_{xx}=0\), giving \(\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\) and \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\) if \(S_{xx}>0\). Centering makes \(\sum(x_i-\bar x)=0\).
  3. Predictions are \(\hat y_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1 x_i\); residuals are actual minus fitted. Thus positive residual means actual exceeds prediction. Intercept OLS yields \(\sum\hat u_i=\sum x_i\hat u_i=0\) as minimization identities; it does not yield \(E[u\mid x]=0\).
  4. For \(y=X\beta+u\), dimensions are \(y, u\):\(n\times 1\); \(X\):\(n\times (k +1)\); \(\beta\):\((k +1)\times 1\). Normal equations \(X'X\hat\beta=X'y\) have \((k +1)\times (k +1)\) multiplying \((k +1)\times 1\). Full column rank makes the inverse available and yields \((X'X)^{-1}X'y=\beta+(X'X)^{-1}X'u\). The equations estimate all coefficients jointly; separate simple regressions do not hold the other variables fixed.
  5. Name the assumption ladder: linear in parameters, random sampling, no perfect collinearity, zero conditional mean, homoskedasticity, conditional normality. A squared/transformed regressor can still be linear in parameters. Algebra needs full rank for uniqueness; sampling properties need additional named assumptions. Zero population conditional mean is about disturbances, not fitted residuals.
sections.title: Explanation steps

sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage OLS estimator and assumptions; fingerprint 8e76f95b0071e8625c31230e9c96e2a738e7d88251b1ba978d0bc35225fc380a. Heading depth alone is adapted.

OLS estimator and assumptions

How does a regression coefficient relate an observed sample to the population relationship we want to study? Week 1 revises ordinary least squares (OLS), then asks which assumptions make its coefficients trustworthy. The formula is a sample calculation; unbiasedness, consistency, and efficiency are properties that require a model of how the data were generated. This distinction prepares the course's later extensions to other data structures. Lecture 1, PDF pp. 10–11

Back to Econometrics II — Week 1.

Population model, sample, and notation

The lecture uses the simple population regression

\[y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+u_i,\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.\]

Here \(i\) labels an observation, \(n\) is the sample size, \(y_i\) is the dependent variable, and \(x_i\) is one explanatory variable. The population parameters \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) describe the intercept and slope. The disturbance \(u_i\) collects the variation in \(y_i\) that the specified systematic part does not explain. A hat indicates a sample estimator or its realized estimate, so \(\hat\beta_1\) differs conceptually from the fixed population parameter \(\beta_1\). Lecture 1, PDF pp. 14–15

The slope measures the change in the systematic part of \(y\) associated with a one-unit change in \(x\). Its units are units of \(y\) per unit of \(x\). The intercept is the systematic value at \(x=0\); interpreting it substantively requires that zero be meaningful and relevant to the data. A causal interpretation of the slope requires appropriate assumptions about the disturbance and regressor; the existence of a fitted line by itself does not establish causation. These interpretations unpack the model used in the lecture and the units-and-parameters task in the seminar. Lecture 1, PDF p. 14; Seminar 1, PDF p. 1, Problem 1(ii)

How OLS chooses the line

Algebraic explanation of the lecture's estimator. OLS selects coefficients \(b_0,b_1\) to minimize the sum of squared residuals,

\[Q(b_0,b_1)=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-b_0-b_1x_i)^2.\]

Differentiating with respect to \(b_0\) and \(b_1\) gives the two normal equations: \(\sum_i(y_i-b_0-b_1x_i)=0\) and \(\sum_ix_i(y_i-b_0-b_1x_i)=0\). The first equation implies \(b_0=\bar y-b_1\bar x\). Substituting this into the second equation produces the centered formula shown in the lecture:

\[\hat\beta_1=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}} =\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)} {\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2}, \qquad \hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x.\]

The bars denote sample means. The numerator measures how \(x\) and \(y\) vary together around their means; the denominator measures the sample variation available in \(x\). The slope therefore compares co-movement with regressor variation. If every \(x_i\) is identical, \(S_{xx}=0\), so the data cannot distinguish the slope from the intercept. The minimization steps are an agent explanation of the displayed source formula, rather than additional lecture slides. Lecture 1, PDF p. 15

The fitted value is \(\hat y_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i\) and the residual is \(\hat u_i=y_i-\hat y_i\). Residuals are observable after estimation; population disturbances are generally unobserved. With an intercept, the normal equations ensure \(\sum_i\hat u_i=0\) and \(\sum_ix_i\hat u_i=0\). These are fitting identities and do not establish the population exogeneity assumption \(E[u_i\mid x_i]=0\). The seminar asks for residuals precisely because they can be calculated from the observed data and fitted line. Seminar 1, PDF p. 1, Problem 1(iv); Lecture 1, PDF p. 18

The assumption ladder

The lecture uses Wooldridge's numbering. State the assumptions by name as well as number, because different textbooks number them differently. The following notation makes the lecture's named assumptions explicit. For multiple regression let \(x_i=(x_{i1},\ldots,x_{ik})\) contain the \(k\) nonconstant regressors, and let \(X\) denote the full sample design, including an intercept. Lecture 1, PDF p. 18; Lecture 1, PDF p. 25

Assumption Meaning and role
Linear in parameters (MLR.1) \(y_i=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^k\beta_jx_{ij}+u_i\). Linearity refers to the coefficients: a regressor can itself be a transformation, provided the specified model remains linear in its parameters. This supplies the decomposition used in the estimator proofs.
Random sampling (MLR.2) Observations are independent draws from the population under study. The lecture emphasizes representativeness and independence. This justifies the cross-sectional sampling argument and the law-of-large-numbers reasoning used later. A convenience sample is not made representative by running OLS.
No perfect collinearity (MLR.3) No regressor is an exact linear combination of the others, and each nonconstant regressor has variation. In simple regression this requires \(S_{xx}>0\); in multiple regression it makes the design matrix full rank. Otherwise coefficients cannot be uniquely separated.
Zero conditional mean (MLR.4) \(E[u_i\mid x_{i1},\ldots,x_{ik}]=0\). Once the included regressors are fixed, the average disturbance is zero. Under the sampling assumptions this yields \(E[u_i\mid X]=0\) in the source's conditional proof.
Homoskedasticity (MLR.5) \(\operatorname{Var}(u_i\mid x_i)=\sigma^2\), a constant finite variance. With the preceding assumptions, this establishes the Gauss–Markov efficiency result.
Normality (MLR.6) The disturbance has a conditional normal distribution; together with the preceding assumptions, this gives normal conditional coefficient distributions and exact null \(t\) and \(F\) distributions.

The lecture introduces the first four assumptions for unbiasedness, adds homoskedasticity for BLUE, and adds normality for classical finite-sample inference. The formal statements here explain that sequence; they should not be read as claims that the seminar data automatically satisfy it. Lecture 1, PDF pp. 16–19; Lecture 1, PDF pp. 23–26

Why multiple regression uses matrix notation

The lecture asks why matrix notation is more convenient when there is more than one regressor. Agent explanation: write \(y=X\beta+u\), where \(y\) and \(u\) are \(n\times1\) vectors, \(X\) is \(n\times(k+1)\), and \(\beta\) is \((k+1)\times1\). Its first column is ones. Minimizing \((y-Xb)'(y-Xb)\) yields \(X'X\hat\beta=X'y\). If \(X\) has full column rank,

\[\hat\beta=(X'X)^{-1}X'y =\beta+(X'X)^{-1}X'u.\]

The prime means transpose. The inverse exists under no perfect collinearity. This single expression handles every coefficient jointly, instead of treating each regressor as a separate simple regression. Joint estimation matters because the slope for a regressor holds the other included regressors fixed; omitting them generally changes the comparison being made. This is the extension requested in the seminar's alternative-specification table. Lecture 1, PDF p. 15, matrix-notation question; Seminar 1, PDF p. 2, Problem 1(vi)–(vii)

What to carry forward

OLS always describes a calculation once the data and specification are fixed. The assumption ladder determines what can be concluded about repeated samples, large samples, relative precision, and hypothesis tests. Unbiasedness, consistency, and efficiency (unbiasedness; consistency; efficiency and inference) proves these distinctions using the estimator's disturbance term. The transport-demand seminar (ten-city calculation; CSV analysis and report; diagnostics) applies the calculation and shows why a change in controls can change the estimated price relationship.

The intercept is held at \(0.5\), so this plot changes only the slope. It does not refit both coefficients and supplies no evidence of exogeneity or causality.

interactions.prompt_html: Move the slope and watch the vertical residuals and their sum of squares.
interactions.solution_html: With the intercept fixed at \(0.5\), the squared residuals sum to \(Q(b)=0.25+(1.5-b)^2+(5.5-2b)^2\). Hence \(Q^{\prime}(b)=10b-25\), which is zero at \(b=2.5\). The fitted values are \((0.5,3,5.5)\), and the residuals are \((0.5,-1,0.5)\).

interactions.prompt_html: At intercept \(0.5\) and slope \(2.5\), what is the sum of squared residuals?
interactions.solution_html: Square and add: \(0.5^2+(-1)^2+0.5^2=1.5\). The sum is measured in squared units of the response. This is an illustrative calculation, not an assessed result.

sections.html:
Derive the slope disturbance decomposition and conditional/unconditional mean, identify the role of each first four assumption, and explain the limits of repeated-sample unbiasedness. The question is what the available information lets us calculate or conclude, and which extra conditions the conclusion needs.

Unbiasedness means \(E[\hat\beta_j]=\beta_j\) across repeated samples. Conditioning on \(X\) fixes weights/denominator. It does not fix disturbances or set each realized disturbance to zero. The first four named assumptions suffice; homoskedasticity and normality are not required for this mean result.
sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
1. From the linear population equation subtract sample means: \(y_i-\bar y=\beta_1(x_i-\bar x)+(u_i-\bar u)\).
  2. Insert into \(S_{xy}/S_{xx}\); cancel \(\beta_1 S_{xx}/S_{xx}\). Since centered \(x\) sums \(0\), the term involving \(\bar u\) vanishes: \(\hat\beta_1=\beta_1+\sum(x_i-\bar x)u_i/S_{xx}\).
  3. Conditional on the whole sample \(X, S_{xx}\) and centered weights are fixed. Thus \(E[\hat\beta_1\mid X]=\beta_1+S_{xx}^{-1}\sum(x_i-\bar x)E[u_i\mid X]\). Random sampling plus observation-level zero conditional mean supply \(E[u_i\mid X]=0\).
  4. The mean error term is \(0\). Iterated expectation gives \(E[\hat\beta_1]=E[E[\hat\beta_1\mid X]]=\beta_1\). For all coefficients, the note's matrix decomposition gives the same conditional argument \(E[\hat\beta\mid X]=\beta+(X'X)^{-1}X'E[u\mid X]=\beta\).
  5. Linear parameters allow decomposition; random sampling supports conditioning on the full sample; no perfect collinearity allows finite inverse/positive denominator; zero conditional mean eliminates mean errors. Homoskedasticity controls variance, not this mean; normality supports exact inference later.
  6. Realized estimation error generally remains nonzero. An unbiased estimator can have large dispersion; one coefficient, residual orthogonality or a high fit cannot certify its repeated-sample property.
sections.title: Explanation steps

sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage One decomposition drives both proofs; fingerprint afc4f90940a6f9e889acff6e5e1194c5fde424636cbfca31f540eee2c5051595. Heading depth alone is adapted.

One decomposition drives both proofs

For \(y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+u_i\), centering gives \(y_i-\bar y=\beta_1(x_i-\bar x)+(u_i-\bar u)\). Substitute this into the OLS numerator:

\[\begin{aligned} \hat\beta_1 &=\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)[\beta_1(x_i-\bar x)+(u_i-\bar u)]}{S_{xx}}\\ &=\beta_1+\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(u_i-\bar u)}{S_{xx}}\\ &=\beta_1+\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)u_i}{S_{xx}}. \end{aligned}\]

The final step uses \(\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=0\), so subtracting \(\bar u\) changes nothing. This algebra identifies the estimation error: sample co-movement between the regressor and disturbance, divided by sample regressor variation. The lecture uses the uncentered-disturbance version for unbiasedness and the centered version for consistency. Lecture 1, PDF p. 19; Lecture 1, PDF p. 22

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Unbiasedness: the repeated-sample average; fingerprint afc4f90940a6f9e889acff6e5e1194c5fde424636cbfca31f540eee2c5051595. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Unbiasedness: the repeated-sample average

An estimator is unbiased when \(E[\hat\beta_j]=\beta_j\). Expectation refers to repeated sampling from the population under the model, not to averaging different coefficients from a single fitted regression. The lecture's theorem states that the linear-in-parameters, random-sampling, no-perfect-collinearity, and zero-conditional-mean assumptions imply unbiasedness for all OLS coefficients. Homoskedasticity and normality are not required for this result. Lecture 1, PDF pp. 16–18

To see the role of exogeneity, condition on the observed regressor sample \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\). Then \(S_{xx}\) and the weights \(x_i-\bar x\) are fixed. Linearity of conditional expectation gives

\[E[\hat\beta_1\mid X] =\beta_1+\frac{1}{S_{xx}}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)E[u_i\mid X] =\beta_1.\]

The zero-conditional-mean assumption, together with random sampling, supplies \(E[u_i\mid X]=0\). Taking expectation again gives \(E[\hat\beta_1]=E[E[\hat\beta_1\mid X]]=\beta_1\). Linearity of the model supplies the initial decomposition; no perfect collinearity makes the denominator positive; random sampling supports the move from observation-level exogeneity to conditioning on the full sample design. Lecture 1, PDF p. 19, conditional-expectation derivation

Source crop: Lecture 1, PDF p. 19. The weights and denominator can leave the conditional expectation because \(X\) is held fixed; exogeneity makes the remaining conditional disturbance means zero. Source, PDF p. 19

Unbiasedness means there is no systematic overestimation or underestimation across repeated samples. It does not guarantee that the estimate from a particular sample is close to the truth: dispersion can be large even when its center is correct. That is why precision and consistency are separate questions. Lecture 1, PDF p. 17

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage The assumption ladder; fingerprint 8e76f95b0071e8625c31230e9c96e2a738e7d88251b1ba978d0bc35225fc380a. Heading depth alone is adapted.

The assumption ladder

The lecture uses Wooldridge's numbering. State the assumptions by name as well as number, because different textbooks number them differently. The following notation makes the lecture's named assumptions explicit. For multiple regression let \(x_i=(x_{i1},\ldots,x_{ik})\) contain the \(k\) nonconstant regressors, and let \(X\) denote the full sample design, including an intercept. Lecture 1, PDF p. 18; Lecture 1, PDF p. 25

Assumption Meaning and role
Linear in parameters (MLR.1) \(y_i=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^k\beta_jx_{ij}+u_i\). Linearity refers to the coefficients: a regressor can itself be a transformation, provided the specified model remains linear in its parameters. This supplies the decomposition used in the estimator proofs.
Random sampling (MLR.2) Observations are independent draws from the population under study. The lecture emphasizes representativeness and independence. This justifies the cross-sectional sampling argument and the law-of-large-numbers reasoning used later. A convenience sample is not made representative by running OLS.
No perfect collinearity (MLR.3) No regressor is an exact linear combination of the others, and each nonconstant regressor has variation. In simple regression this requires \(S_{xx}>0\); in multiple regression it makes the design matrix full rank. Otherwise coefficients cannot be uniquely separated.
Zero conditional mean (MLR.4) \(E[u_i\mid x_{i1},\ldots,x_{ik}]=0\). Once the included regressors are fixed, the average disturbance is zero. Under the sampling assumptions this yields \(E[u_i\mid X]=0\) in the source's conditional proof.
Homoskedasticity (MLR.5) \(\operatorname{Var}(u_i\mid x_i)=\sigma^2\), a constant finite variance. With the preceding assumptions, this establishes the Gauss–Markov efficiency result.
Normality (MLR.6) The disturbance has a conditional normal distribution; together with the preceding assumptions, this gives normal conditional coefficient distributions and exact null \(t\) and \(F\) distributions.

The lecture introduces the first four assumptions for unbiasedness, adds homoskedasticity for BLUE, and adds normality for classical finite-sample inference. The formal statements here explain that sequence; they should not be read as claims that the seminar data automatically satisfy it. Lecture 1, PDF pp. 16–19; Lecture 1, PDF pp. 23–26

O003-W v1, hypothetical fixed \(X=(1,2,3), \beta_1=2, S_{xx}=2\). A realized \(u=(1,0,3)\) gives centered weighted sum \((-1)(1)+0+(1)(3)=2\); \(\text{slope}=3\). This single error of \(+1\) does not refute a model whose repeated-sample conditional \(u\) means are \(0\). Under those mean assumptions \(E[\text{slope}\mid X]=2+(-1\cdot0+0\cdot0+1\cdot0)/2=2\), then \(E[\text{slope}]=2\). Compare realized \(u\) with its conditional expectation: no step requires all realized \(u\) to vanish.

Role: complete demonstration, never independent evidence. Unless explicitly identified as a finished-note result, numerical/context examples are agent-created hypothetical instantiations of the note-supported mechanism.

O003-S

item_id: O003-S, item_version: 1, role: supported_completion, condition: supported, relation: parallel_variant.

Prompt: Complete centered \(y\) expression, disturbance decomposition, conditional expectation and iterated expectation. For \(X=(1,2,3), \beta_1=2, S_{xx}=2\), explain why realized weighted \(u\) sum \(2\) gives \(\text{slope}=3\) but conditional means \(0\) give expected \(\text{slope}=2\). interactions.solution_html:

Realized \(\text{slope}=2+2/2=3\); \(\text{conditional expectation}=2+\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)0/2=2\); iterated expectation \(2\). First four: linear parameters, random sampling, no perfect collinearity, zero conditional mean. Normality is irrelevant to setting the conditional mean \(0\); realization need not equal mean. Matrix counterpart: \(E[\hat\beta\mid X]=\beta+(X^{\top}X)^{-1}X^{\top}E[u\mid X]=\beta\).

Sign: expectation of ratio treated as ratio of expectations without conditioning, or claims unbiasedness makes each error \(0\). Correction: fix \(X\) to make the denominator and weights constants; exogeneity sets conditional disturbance means, not realizations, to \(0\). Hint1: what is fixed conditional on \(X\)? Score the original response before help. One ambiguous error only suggests a tentative misconception; establish it only from explicit reasoning or repeated diagnostic signs. Explain the relevant prepared step and its consequence; never label the learner from confidence or a single slip.

Study conditions, assessment scope and sources

Required components (all must be elicited and passed):

  • C1: Normalized centered ratio and justified probability limit with correct target.
  • C2: States sampling/finite moments/positive finite denominator and weaker intercept/slope moments.
  • C3: Precise fixed \(\epsilon\) probability definition and larger-\(n\) limitation.
  • C4: Correct Chebyshev bound and nuanced unbiasedness/bias/dispersion distinction.

Finished-note authority:

sections.title: Prerequisites and checks

sections.html:
Derive the probability limit from centered OLS, state sampling/moment/nondegeneracy and orthogonality conditions, and discriminate finite-sample unbiasedness from concentration in probability. The question is what the available information lets us calculate or conclude, and which extra conditions the conclusion needs.

Consistency is \(\hat\theta_n\to_p\theta\): for every fixed \(\epsilon>0\), \(P(|\text{estimate}-\text{target}|>\epsilon)\to0\). It concerns a sequence indexed by \(n\), not monotonic improvement of every realized sample. Probability limit names the value around which the sequence concentrates; it may differ from the intended parameter.
sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
1. Use \(\hat\beta_1=\beta_1+\frac{n^{-1}\sum(x_i-\bar x)(u_i-\bar u)}{n^{-1}\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2}\), obtained by centered substitution and common division by \(n\).
  2. Under independent random sampling and finite moments sufficient for the law of large numbers, sample covariance tends to \(\operatorname{Cov}(x, u)\), sample variance to \(\operatorname{Var}(x)\). Require positive finite population \(\operatorname{Var}(x)\) so the ratio is valid. Then \(\operatorname{plim}\text{slope}=\beta_1+\operatorname{Cov}(x,u)/\operatorname{Var}(x)\).
  3. If covariance \(0\) the slope limit equals \(\beta_1\); otherwise larger samples concentrate at the wrong target. Zero conditional mean is sufficient, stronger than needed for these moments. The weaker condition is \(E[u]=0\) for the intercept and \(\operatorname{Cov}(x_j,u)=0\) for every nonconstant regressor, alongside other model/sampling/moment/rank conditions. \(\operatorname{Cov}(1,u)=0\) says nothing about \(E[u]\).
  4. Finite-sample unbiasedness concerns an expectation at each \(n\). Consistency concerns concentration. Neither follows from one estimate or an unqualified large \(n\).
  5. For an unbiased sequence, Chebyshev bounds \(P(|\widehat\theta-\theta|>\epsilon)\leq\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\theta)/\epsilon^2\); if variance \(\to 0\), the probability bound \(\to 0\). Unbiasedness alone does not require variance shrinkage. A finite-sample biased sequence can be consistent if error/bias disappears with \(n\) and its sampling error concentrates; do not infer consistency solely from decreasing bias without controlling dispersion.
sections.title: Explanation steps

sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Consistency: concentration as sample size grows; fingerprint afc4f90940a6f9e889acff6e5e1194c5fde424636cbfca31f540eee2c5051595. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Consistency: concentration as sample size grows

Consistency is convergence in probability: \(\hat\beta_{j,n}\xrightarrow{p}\beta_j\). More explicitly, for every fixed tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\),

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}P(|\hat\beta_{j,n}-\beta_j|>\varepsilon)=0.\]

The subscript \(n\) emphasizes a sequence of estimators indexed by sample size. Consistency says that the probability of an error larger than any fixed tolerance approaches zero. It does not promise monotonic improvement for every realized sequence of samples. The lecture states OLS consistency under the first four assumptions and then shows that zero conditional mean is stronger than necessary for this particular large-sample result. Lecture 1, PDF pp. 20–21

Why population covariance determines the probability limit

Divide both parts of the disturbance ratio by \(n\):

\[\hat\beta_1=\beta_1+ \frac{n^{-1}\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(u_i-\bar u)} {n^{-1}\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2}.\]

Under random sampling and finite moments sufficient for the law of large numbers, the numerator converges in probability to \(\operatorname{Cov}(x,u)\) and the denominator to \(\operatorname{Var}(x)\). With a positive finite population regressor variance, taking the ratio therefore gives

\[\operatorname{plim}\hat\beta_1 =\beta_1+\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(x,u)}{\operatorname{Var}(x)}.\]

Here \(\operatorname{plim}\) means probability limit. Finite moments and a nonzero limiting denominator are the regularity requirements needed to interpret the lecture's law-of-large-numbers step; the slide does not spell them out. If \(\operatorname{Cov}(x,u)=0\), the additional term vanishes. If it is nonzero, more observations concentrate OLS around the wrong value. A larger sample therefore cannot by itself cure regressor–disturbance correlation. Lecture 1, PDF p. 22, probability-limit derivation

Source crop: Lecture 1, PDF p. 22. Centering and division by \(n\) turn the estimation-error ratio into sample covariance over sample variance, which exposes its population limit. Source, PDF p. 22

A weaker exogeneity condition

For consistency, the lecture replaces zero conditional mean by the weaker conditions

\[E[u]=0, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(x_j,u)=0\quad\text{for each nonconstant regressor }j=1,\ldots,k.\]

The first condition handles the intercept, and the covariance conditions handle the slopes. The slide writes its index as \(j=0,\ldots,k\); with a constant regressor \(x_0=1\), its covariance with \(u\) is automatically zero. This weaker condition, together with the other sampling, model, nondegeneracy, and moment conditions, supports consistency but need not imply finite-sample unbiasedness. Zero conditional mean implies these unconditional moments, whereas unconditional zero covariance need not imply a zero conditional mean at every regressor value. Lecture 1, PDF p. 21

How unbiasedness and consistency can differ

The lecture states that an unbiased estimator is consistent if its variance tends to zero. Agent explanation: when \(E[\hat\theta_n]=\theta\), Chebyshev's inequality bounds \(P(|\hat\theta_n-\theta|>\varepsilon)\) by \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_n)/\varepsilon^2\), so a vanishing variance implies convergence in probability. Unbiasedness alone does not control the variance. Conversely, finite-sample bias can vanish as \(n\) grows, so a biased estimator can still be consistent. These are properties of the sampling sequence, not a classification that can be proved by examining one estimate. Lecture 1, PDF p. 21

sections.html:
O004-W v1, hypothetical \(\beta_1=-2, \operatorname{Cov}(x, u)=3, \operatorname{Var}(x)=6\) with the note's regularity: \(\text{plim}=-2+3/6=-1.5\). Population correlation contributes \(+0.5\), so more data do not recover \(-2\). Separately, an unbiased sequence with \(\operatorname{Var}=4/n\) and \(\epsilon=0.5\) has error probability \(\le (4/n)/(0.25)=16/n\), tending \(0\) (a bound may exceed \(1\) for small \(n\) without becoming a probability claim). This is an application of the finished note's Chebyshev explanation, not a new theorem.

Role: complete demonstration, never independent evidence. Unless explicitly identified as a finished-note result, numerical/context examples are agent-created hypothetical instantiations of the note-supported mechanism.

Self-assessment criteria and tutor checks

Pass: all C1–C4 correct, essential reasoning explicit, known independent conditions and fresh item. Partial: one or more components missing, an unexplained claim, or a recoverable arithmetic slip with sound method. Fail: a critical conceptual error, wrong method/assumptions/interpretation, or no usable attempt. Unscorable: unknown conditions/exposure or an alternative outside the prepared key. Equivalent algebra, clear verbal reasoning and synonymous units/assumption names are acceptable; assumption numbers alone are insufficient. Numerical rounding to sensible precision is acceptable. A isolated arithmetic slip is partial and is not treated as established conceptual failure; the learner must independently repair it with a fresh prepared full item before a pass qualifies. No numeric grading scale is invented.

Every full task I1, I2, D1, D2 expressly requests all C1–C4 and has a complete task-specific key plus exact conceptual reasoning above. Omitted pieces are partial even if an unasked answer happens to sound fluent. Supported S and narrow correction C never substitute for a full check.

Permitted acquisition routes: I1+I2; if an item was exposed, failed or unavailable, replace only that full check with a previously unexposed D1 or D2. Any selected pair of distinct items from {I1,I2,D1,D2} covers C1–C4 twice. Do not use an item twice or count a corrected answer to the same item as fresh. D items used immediately are logged as independent replacement checks, not delayed evidence. No shortened variant or arbitrary new task is permitted. Two complete unassisted passes under O004-C1 establish acquisition; they do not establish retention. This is a default evidence rule, not a learner outcome.

sections.html:
Sign: “large samples cure endogeneity”, “unbiased implies consistent”, or treating covariance \(0\) as conditional mean \(0\). Correction: the LLN retains \(\operatorname{Cov}(x,u)/\operatorname{Var}(x)\); concentration needs a correct limit, while finite-sample unbiasedness alone gives no shrinking-error guarantee. Hint1: identify numerator/denominator limits. Hint2: add their ratio to \(\beta\).

Score the original response before help. One ambiguous error only suggests a tentative misconception; establish it only from explicit reasoning or repeated diagnostic signs. Explain the relevant prepared step and its consequence; never label the learner from confidence or a single slip.

sections.html:
Derive the simple-slope conditional variance, state the precise BLUE comparison class, calculate a conventional slope standard error/\(t\) statistic and degrees of freedom, and discriminate which assumptions support each property. The question is what the available information lets us calculate or conclude, and which extra conditions the conclusion needs.

BLUE means best linear unbiased estimator conditional on \(X\). Linear means linear in \(y\) observations with \(X\)-determined weights; unbiased is the comparison restriction; best is minimum conditional variance within that class, coefficient by coefficient. It is not minimum variance among all estimators/all loss functions. Homoskedasticity is common finite conditional disturbance variance \(\sigma^2\). Normality is additional for the stated exact finite-sample null \(t\) and \(F\) distributions; \(F\) addresses joint coefficient restrictions, whose calculation is outside this bounded lesson.
sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
1. In the slope decomposition the error is a weighted sum of \(u\) with weights \((x_i-\bar x)/S_{xx}\). Variance of this sum has squared weight variance terms and cross-observation covariance terms.
  2. Sampling conditions remove the cross terms; common conditional variance \(\sigma^2\) gives \(Var(\hat\beta_1\mid X)=\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2\sigma^2/S_{xx}^2=\sigma^2/S_{xx}\). More \(x\) variation improves precision, more noise worsens it.
  3. With MLR1–5, the Gauss–Markov theorem gives BLUE in the stated linear unbiased class; this explanation calculates OLS variance, not a full proof of the theorem. No normality needed for BLUE.
  4. Estimate unknown \(\sigma^2\) by \(SSE/(n-k -1)\), giving simple-slope estimated variance \(\hat\sigma^2/S_{xx}\) and \(\mathrm{se}\) its square root. \(k\) counts nonconstant regressors: residual \(\mathrm{df}=n-k -1\), not \(n-k\).
  5. For null \(\beta_{1,0}\) use \(t=(\text{estimated slope}-\text{null})/\mathrm{se}\). Under the full six classical assumptions, compare to the \(t\) distribution with those \(\mathrm{df}\) for exact finite-sample inference. Rejecting a zero slope does not establish exogeneity/causality. An \(F\) test addresses joint restrictions; no joint-test arithmetic is claimed without further prepared notes.
  6. With heteroskedasticity but first four assumptions maintained, unbiasedness survives and consistency may survive with regularity; stated BLUE/conventional variance and exact classical \(t\) claims no longer follow. With MLR1–5 but nonnormality, BLUE still holds while the stated exact classical normal/\(t\)/\(F\) distributions are not established. This lesson supplies no unsupported replacement variance/test method.
sections.title: Explanation steps

sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Efficiency: specify the comparison class; fingerprint afc4f90940a6f9e889acff6e5e1194c5fde424636cbfca31f540eee2c5051595. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Efficiency: specify the comparison class

The Gauss–Markov theorem says that under linearity in parameters, random sampling, no perfect collinearity, zero conditional mean, and homoskedasticity, OLS is BLUE conditional on \(X\): the best linear unbiased estimator. “Linear” means linear in the dependent-variable observations, with weights determined by \(X\). “Unbiased” restricts the comparison to estimators centered on the target parameter. “Best” means smallest conditional variance within that class, coefficient by coefficient. This does not claim that every conceivable estimator has a larger variance, or that OLS minimizes all possible loss functions. Lecture 1, PDF pp. 23–24

For the simple-regression slope, the decomposition provides an explanatory variance calculation. Under conditional independence and common disturbance variance \(\sigma^2\),

\[\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1\mid X) =\frac{1}{S_{xx}^2}\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2\sigma^2 =\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}.\]

Cross-observation covariance terms vanish under the sampling assumptions. More variation in \(x\) supplies a more precise slope, while more disturbance variation reduces precision. This equation answers the seminar's slope-variance question and explains why homoskedasticity matters for the usual standard error. With heteroskedasticity, zero conditional mean can still preserve unbiasedness and suitable conditions can preserve consistency, but the stated BLUE theorem and conventional variance formula no longer follow. Lecture 1, PDF p. 24; Seminar 1, PDF p. 2, slope-variance task

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Normality and hypothesis tests add another requirement; fingerprint afc4f90940a6f9e889acff6e5e1194c5fde424636cbfca31f540eee2c5051595. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Normality and hypothesis tests add another requirement

The lecture adds normality to the preceding assumptions to obtain a conditional normal distribution for OLS coefficients and exact null \(t\) and \(F\) distributions. This is a finite-sample inference statement, separate from unbiasedness, consistency, and BLUE. For a null slope value \(\beta_{1,0}\),

\[t=\frac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_{1,0}}{\operatorname{se}(\hat\beta_1)}.\]

Under the classical assumptions, in a regression with \(k\) nonconstant regressors this statistic has a \(t\) distribution with \(n-k-1\) residual degrees of freedom under the null. An \(F\) statistic addresses joint coefficient restrictions. The formula and degrees of freedom are an agent expansion of the lecture's null-distribution statement, used in the seminar's requested slope test. A small standard error or a large absolute \(t\) statistic cannot establish exogeneity; inference is conditional on the maintained model assumptions. Lecture 1, PDF pp. 25–26; Seminar 1, PDF p. 2

Origin: reused complete checked passage Distinctions to retain; fingerprint afc4f90940a6f9e889acff6e5e1194c5fde424636cbfca31f540eee2c5051595. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Distinctions to retain

Question Property Week 1 OLS conditions and qualification
Is the repeated-sample center correct? Unbiasedness First four assumptions; an individual estimate can still be far from the parameter.
Does error become improbable as \(n\) grows? Consistency First four assumptions are sufficient with regularity; weaker orthogonality moments can replace zero conditional mean.
Is the estimator most precise in the stated class? BLUE efficiency First five assumptions; the class is linear unbiased estimators conditional on \(X\).
Are the stated finite-sample null distributions exact? Classical inference First six assumptions; normality is an additional requirement.

These distinctions summarize Lecture 1, PDF pp. 16–26. The transport-demand seminar (ten-city calculation; CSV analysis and report; diagnostics) turns them into interpretation questions: fit the model, identify what the evidence measures, and assess which assumptions can plausibly support it.

The question is what the available information lets us calculate or conclude, and which extra conditions the conclusion needs.

A fare-demand linear specification imposes a constant fitted change per fare unit. Expected negative fare sign is a starting hypothesis, not a source-mandated law. Potential omitted factors include population/density, service quality, car availability, income/driving cost; if they affect demand and co-vary with fare, zero conditional mean can fail. The ten-city table explicitly labels \(y\) as passengers per hour(thousand), \(x\) dollars: preserve this literal scale even when surprising. sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
1. Specify \(\mathrm{travel}=\beta_0+\beta_1\mathrm{fare}+u\); interpret slope in \(y\)-units per dollar, zero-fare intercept only if relevant. Fix the dataset before calculation; never import CSV units into the table.
  2. Obtain mean \(x\), mean \(y\), \(S_{xx}\), \(S_{xy}\); divide \(S_{xy}/S_{xx}\) and solve intercept. Use fitted difference \(\text{slope}\cdot\text{fare change}\) rather than percentage language for a level-level model.
  3. For each city compute fitted and actual-minus-fitted. Check residual sum and fare-weighted residual sum \(\approx 0\), allowing rounding. These are fitting checks, not assumption evidence.
  4. \(SSE\) is sum of squared fitted residuals; divide by \(n -2\) for simple regression with intercept. Slope variance estimate \(\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta_1)=\hat\sigma^2/S_{xx}\); \(\mathrm{se}\) is square root; \(t=\text{slope}/\mathrm{se}\) for zero null. Under all six assumptions compare \(\lvert t\rvert\) with the appropriate two-sided critical value from the \(t_{n-2}\) distribution; report nonrejection as uncertainty, not proof of no association.
  5. Inspect impossible fitted values, very large residuals and intercept extrapolation. The ten-city negative fitted travel at observed fare \(1.50\) signals linear-specification limitations. It does not license deleting observations. Economic explanations are hypotheses requiring evidence.
  6. Interpret the result as sample association unless exogeneity/sampling conditions are supported. Regression alone cannot choose an optimal fare.
sections.title: Explanation steps

sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage From economic intuition to a model; fingerprint 8cb7c6b76f548352c216ae9bd1d909a788d8d8f5b8718c2721d23989ce332d7f. Heading depth alone is adapted.

From economic intuition to a model

Problem 1(i) asks about the sign and shape of demand and other influences. A plausible starting hypothesis is that a higher fare reduces public-transport use, holding relevant alternatives and service conditions fixed. A straight line imposes a constant change in demand per unit price; a curved or logarithmic relation would impose a different shape. The handout leaves the shape to discussion, so the linear model used below is a transparent choice for revising OLS, not a source-mandated demand law. Seminar 1, PDF p. 1, Problem 1(i)–(iii)

An initial specification is

\[\text{travel}_i=\beta_0+\beta_1\text{price}_i+u_i.\]

The slope is the change in the model's systematic travel demand associated with a one-unit increase in fare. The intercept is its value at zero fare. Other potential influences include city population and density, service frequency and quality, car availability, income, and the cost of driving. These are economic hypotheses offered to answer the prompt, not variables all observed in the supplied data. If such factors both affect demand and vary systematically with fare, putting them in \(u_i\) can violate zero conditional mean. A negative estimated price coefficient alone therefore does not identify a causal demand curve. Seminar 1, PDF p. 1, Problem 1(i)–(ii); Lecture 1, PDF p. 18, exogeneity

The manager's ultimate objective is an optimal fare, but the exercise only estimates demand and evaluates the regression. Choosing an optimal fare would additionally require a defined objective, costs or capacity constraints, and a credible estimate of how fare changes affect demand. Those inputs are not supplied; no optimum is claimed here. This limitation follows from the distinction between the manager's motivating question and the tasks actually specified in Problem 1. Seminar 1, PDF p. 1

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Ten-city example: keep the source's measurement scale; fingerprint 8cb7c6b76f548352c216ae9bd1d909a788d8d8f5b8718c2721d23989ce332d7f. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Ten-city example: keep the source's measurement scale

The printed table labels the dependent variable “Passengers per hour (thousand)” and the fare “Fair price (dollars).” The values below preserve the printed numbers literally. The large passenger scale is not silently corrected. Thus a unit of \(y\) means one unit on the table's stated thousand-passengers-per-hour scale, and a unit of price means one dollar. The later CSV has a different numeric scale and no supplied unit dictionary, so its results must not be assigned these table units automatically. Seminar 1, PDF p. 1, city table

Source crop: the original ten-city table, including its unit labels. It supplies the observations for the following calculations. Source, PDF p. 1

Estimate the line

For the ten cities, the calculated sample means and centered sums are

\[\bar x=0.93,\qquad\bar y=1894,\qquad S_{xx}=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2=1.031,\]

\[S_{xy}=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)=-3579.7.\]

Applying the lecture's OLS formula gives

\[\hat\beta_1=\frac{-3579.7}{1.031}=-3472.065955, \qquad \hat\beta_0=1894-(-3472.065955)(0.93)=5123.021339.\]

Hence \(\widehat{\text{travel}}_i=5123.021339-3472.065955\text{price}_i\). A fare difference of $0.10 is associated with a fitted demand difference of \(-347.206596\) units on the printed passenger scale. This is a cross-city association in the chosen linear specification. The estimated intercept is outside the observed fare range, $0.50–$1.50, and should not be interpreted as observed demand under a zero-fare policy. Calculations answer Problem 1(iii) using the source table and Lecture 1's centered estimator. Seminar 1, PDF p. 1; Lecture 1, PDF p. 15

Fitted values and residuals

For each city, calculate \(\hat y_i\) from the fitted line and subtract it from actual travel: \(\hat u_i=y_i-\hat y_i\). Positive residuals mean actual travel exceeds the line's prediction; negative residuals mean actual travel is lower. Rounded results are:

City Printed travel Fare ($) Fitted travel Residual
\(C_1\) 2073 0.85 2171.765 −98.765
\(C_2\) 2136 0.75 2518.972 −382.972
\(C_3\) 1879 0.60 3039.782 −1160.782
\(C_4\) 938 1.00 1650.955 −712.955
\(C_5\) 7343 0.50 3386.988 3956.012
\(C_6\) 838 0.85 2171.765 −1333.765
\(C_7\) 1648 1.00 1650.955 −2.955
\(C_8\) 739 0.75 2518.972 −1779.972
\(C_9\) 1071 1.50 −85.078 1156.078
\(C_{10}\) 275 1.50 −85.078 360.078

The fitted line predicts negative travel at $1.50, illustrating a limitation of this unrestricted linear specification even at an observed fare. The unusually high travel in \(C_5\) also leaves a large positive residual. Neither observation licenses deleting a city; both motivate checking specification and omitted factors. This table is an agent calculation from the source observations, answering Problem 1(iv). Seminar 1, PDF p. 1

Disturbance variance, slope variance, and the t statistic

The true disturbances \(u_i\) and their variance \(\sigma^2\) are unknown. In a simple regression with an intercept, the conventional variance estimator uses \(n-2\) residual degrees of freedom:

\[\hat\sigma^2=\frac{\sum_i\hat u_i^2}{n-2} =\frac{24{,}075{,}579.500}{8} =3{,}009{,}447.437.\]

Two estimated coefficients consume two degrees of freedom. Under the homoskedastic model, the slope's theoretical conditional variance is \(\sigma^2/S_{xx}\); replacing the unknown \(\sigma^2\) with \(\hat\sigma^2\) estimates that variance. The corresponding calculated standard error is

\[\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta_1\mid X)=\frac{\hat\sigma^2}{1.031}, \qquad \operatorname{se}(\hat\beta_1)=1708.496323.\]

For \(H_0:\beta_1=0\), \(t=-3472.065955/1708.496323=-2.032235\). An exact two-sided test compares its absolute value with the appropriate \(t_8\) critical value, under the full classical assumptions. At the conventional 5% level it does not reject zero: \(|t|\) is below the approximately 2.306 critical value. This does not prove no relationship; ten observations and substantial residual variation leave considerable uncertainty. The formulas and computation are the worked solution to the handout's variance and \(t\)-statistic tasks, interpreted using the lecture's inference statement. Seminar 1, PDF pp. 1–2, Problem 1(iv); Lecture 1, PDF p. 26

sections.title: Prerequisites and checks

sections.html:
Interpret the recorded residual plots, compute the note-supported Jarque–Bera and studentized Breusch–Pagan/Koenker statistics, make stated-level decisions from supplied p values, and identify assumptions they cannot establish. The question is what the available information lets us calculate or conclude, and which extra conditions the conclusion needs.

The finished note explicitly selects these diagnostic methods to implement an open-ended seminar task; the handout did not name them. Jarque–Bera uses skewness \(S\) and kurtosis \(K\) with normal benchmarks \(0\) and \(3\). Homoskedasticity is constant conditional disturbance variance; the studentized BP/Koenker auxiliary regression explains squared residuals by an intercept and selected regressors. These are large-sample tests with their own conditions, not exact proofs of population assumptions.
sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
1. Inspect residual histogram/normal Q–Q plot: diagonal compatibility supports a normal-shaped description; curvature/tail departures raise concerns. The recorded plot is broadly symmetric/near diagonal with some tails. Residuals are estimated disturbances constrained by OLS, not direct iid draws of true \(u\).
  2. Centered residual moments \(m_r=n^{-1}\sum_i\hat u_i^r\) yield \(S=m_3/m_2^{3/2}\), \(K=m_4/m_2^2\). \(JB=n[S^2/6+(K-3)^2/24]\), with \(\chi^2_2\) large-sample reference under normal-null/regularity. \(S=0, K=3\) yields \(0\), but matching two moments cannot prove all conditional-distribution properties.
  3. Residuals versus fitted values and squared residuals versus fitted show spread: funnel suggests variance concern. The recorded image has no conspicuous funnel, but a single projection can miss regressor-specific patterns. Regress squared residuals on intercept plus \(q\) nonconstant chosen regressors: \(LM=nR_{\mathrm{aux}}^2\), asymptotic \(\chi^2_q\) under homoskedastic null/independent sampling/moment conditions. \(q\) excludes the intercept; auxiliary specification determines the alternatives probed.
  4. Fix \(\alpha=0.05\) before interpreting supplied \(p\). If \(p<0.05\) reject null; otherwise do not reject. Nonrejection means this test found insufficient contrary evidence; it is not acceptance/proof. No \(p\) value is computed from a invented reference table; prepared \(p\) values are part of the prompts.
  5. Neither diagram/test establishes random sampling, representativeness, population exogeneity, causality or structural definition of the CSV \(u\) column. Sample full rank can establish unique coefficients, but functional form and mean assumptions remain substantive. A good fit and passing diagnostics cannot turn a regression into a causal model.
sections.title: Explanation steps

sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Assumption checks: what diagnostics can establish; fingerprint 8cb7c6b76f548352c216ae9bd1d909a788d8d8f5b8718c2721d23989ce332d7f. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Assumption checks: what diagnostics can establish

Problem 3 requests plots and formal tests of residual normality and homoskedasticity. The following agent-selected diagnostic methods implement that open-ended instruction for model (3). They are not named in the handout. Tests are interpreted at a stated 5% significance level and use large-sample reference distributions; failing to reject is evidence of compatibility, not proof of an assumption. Residuals estimate disturbances and are constrained by OLS fitting, so tests based on them require their own statistical justification. Seminar 1, PDF p. 2, Problem 3

Agent-computed diagnostic plots from all CSV observations for the price–income–gasoline model. The histogram is roughly symmetric; the normal Q–Q plot compares sorted standardized residuals with standard-normal quantiles (red diagonal). Residuals against fitted values show no conspicuous funnel. Squared residuals show the remaining spread more directly. These are calculated visual evidence, not figures in the supplied PDF. Data: travel.csv; Task: Seminar 1, PDF p. 2

Normality: a plot and a moment test

A Q–Q plot matches ordered standardized residuals to normal quantiles: an approximately straight diagonal is compatible with a normal shape, while curvature and tail departures indicate shape differences. The displayed residual histogram is broadly bell-shaped, and the Q–Q points lie near the diagonal, with some tail departures. Neither visual establishes exact conditional normality.

For a formal check, the Jarque–Bera statistic compares sample skewness \(S\) and kurtosis \(K\) with their normal-distribution values of zero and three. Using centered residual moments \(m_r=n^{-1}\sum_i\hat u_i^r\), set \(S=m_3/m_2^{3/2}\) and \(K=m_4/m_2^2\). Residual means are zero apart from numerical rounding because the model has an intercept. The statistic is

\[\mathrm{JB}=n\left(\frac{S^2}{6}+\frac{(K-3)^2}{24}\right).\]

Under the usual large-sample conditions and a normal null, its reference distribution is \(\chi^2_2\). Here \(S=0.031493\), \(K=3.051706\), \(\mathrm{JB}=0.276697\), and the asymptotic \(p\) value is \(0.870795\). We do not reject normality at 5%. This is a selected moment-based check, not proof of all aspects of conditional normality. These definitions and results are the agent's worked method for the source's requested normality test. Seminar 1, PDF p. 2, Problem 3; Calculated from travel.csv

Homoskedasticity: a spread plot and an auxiliary regression

Homoskedasticity means constant conditional disturbance variance. A widening or narrowing residual band against fitted values would raise concerns, while roughly similar spread is compatible with constant variance. The plots show no obvious systematic funnel, but a single projection can miss variance patterns associated with individual regressors.

For a formal check, use an auxiliary regression of squared residuals on an intercept and the three included regressors. The studentized Breusch–Pagan / Koenker form tests whether those regressors explain residual variance. If its \(R^2\) is \(R^2_{\mathrm{aux}}\), its statistic is \(\mathrm{LM}=nR^2_{\mathrm{aux}}\), with a large-sample \(\chi^2_3\) reference under the homoskedastic null and the usual independent-sampling and moment conditions. The three degrees of freedom count the nonconstant auxiliary regressors.

Here \(R^2_{\mathrm{aux}}=0.004737882\), \(\mathrm{LM}=4.737882\), and \(p\approx0.192028\). We do not reject homoskedasticity at 5% against this particular alternative. A different auxiliary specification could detect different variance patterns. This is the agent-selected solution method for the handout's homoskedasticity task, rather than a theorem or test named by the handout. Seminar 1, PDF p. 2, Problem 3; Calculated from travel.csv

Assumptions that remain substantive

The sample design matrix can be checked for full rank; the three CSV specifications have full rank and hence unique OLS coefficients. Functional form remains a modeling choice. The file alone does not document random sampling or representativeness, and residual orthogonality cannot verify population exogeneity. Adding controls may improve a plausible specification, but omitted causes, simultaneity, or measurement error could still invalidate the desired interpretation. Passing residual diagnostics therefore does not prove OLS unbiasedness, consistency, or causality. Those properties follow from the conditions developed in Unbiasedness, consistency, and efficiency (unbiasedness; consistency; efficiency and inference), not from a high \(R^2\). Lecture 1, PDF p. 18; Seminar 1, PDF p. 2, Problems 1(v), 3

Compare same-sample simple/multiple regression output, calculate and interpret ordinary/adjusted \(R^2\), and produce a short empirical report distinguishing conditional association, significance, fit, diagnostics and missing provenance. The question is what the available information lets us calculate or conclude, and which extra conditions the conclusion needs.

Use same dependent variable and observations for the prepared fit comparison. \(SSE\) denotes residual sum of squares here; \(SST=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2\); \(k\) counts nonconstant regressors. With intercept \(R^2=1-SSE/SST\); adjusted \(R^2=1-(SSE/(n-k -1))/(SST/(n -1))\). \(R^2\) describes sample variation around the mean accounted for by the fit, not the causal share or out-of-sample guarantee. CSV 1000 rows has no units, sampling process or generating equation; \(u\)-column name alone gives no structural-error definition.
sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
1. Define research question and choose transparent specification. Simple price model summarizes its bivariate association. Multiple model price slope holds income/gasoline fixed. Read an intercept cautiously at all regressors \(0\) if outside relevant support.
  2. Report \(\text{slope}\cdot\text{one-unit change}\) with units, held-fixed variables and sign. Control-induced slope changes are compatible with omitted-variable effects, not proof the richer model removes all omitted factors. A \(t\) statistic compares estimate with a stated null relative to its conventional \(\mathrm{se}\), conditional on maintained inference assumptions; it is not causal identification/economic importance.
  3. Intercept OLS orthogonality yields \(\text{total}=\text{fitted variation}+SSE\). Hence \(R^2=1-SSE/SST\). Adding regressors to the same sample retains the old fit by setting new coefficients \(0\); minimized \(SSE\) cannot increase, \(R^2\) cannot decrease. Adjusted \(R^2\) penalizes \(\mathrm{df}\); it can fall or be negative. Changes of sample/\(y\) invalidate this simple nesting argument.
  4. Calculate adjusted fit using \(n -1\) versus \(n-k -1\). Never confuse explained sum of squares with \(SSE\) or count the intercept as a nonconstant regressor.
  5. Structure the report: research question, known variables/units and sample/provenance, justified equation, readable coefficient \(+\mathrm{se}\)+fit table, held-fixed interpretations and uncertainty, fit and diagnostic decisions, remaining assumptions and policy limits. Proposed income/private-transport or gasoline/substitution mechanisms are hypotheses, not identified results. Missing \(u\) definition prevents treating it as an ordinary structural control.
  6. This lesson compares already-prepared output/calculations; hands-on R/other-software command competence and raw-data reruns are not assessed by this plan. No optimal fare claim follows without objective/cost/capacity/causal response.

The CSV example: compare specifications

The supplied travel.csv contains 1,000 rows and five numeric columns: travel, price, income, gasoline, and u; all 5,000 data cells are numeric and no entries are missing. No dictionary specifies their units, collection method, population, or generating equation. The column named u is retained in the raw data, but its name alone does not establish that it is an observed structural disturbance or a valid explanatory variable. The models below use the economically interpretable named controls income and gasoline, while preserving u as an undocumented column. This avoids treating unavailable real-world error information as an ordinary control. Seminar 1, PDF p. 2, Problem 1(v)–(vi)

Agent-computed model comparison. Each model has an intercept, uses all 1,000 observations, and is estimated by OLS. Parentheses contain conventional homoskedastic standard errors, not heteroskedasticity-robust ones. Values remain in the CSV's own units.

Interpret conditional associations carefully

In model (3), a one-file-unit increase in price is associated with approximately 2.704 fewer travel units, holding income and gasoline fixed. One additional income unit is associated with 0.150 fewer travel units, holding the other included variables fixed. One additional gasoline unit is associated with 0.811 more travel units. The negative price sign matches the starting hypothesis. A positive gasoline sign is compatible with more expensive driving making public transport relatively attractive. A negative income sign is compatible with substitution toward private transport as income rises, although this is a proposed mechanism, not a mechanism identified by these estimates. The dataset's unknown units prevent interpretation as dollars, percentages, or a particular number of passengers. Seminar 1, PDF p. 2, interpretation prompt; Computed from travel.csv

The price slope becomes much less negative after income is included. The specifications answer different questions: model (1) summarizes unconditional price–travel association, whereas models (2) and (3) compare observations at the same included control values. The change is compatible with omitted-variable effects in the simple model; it does not prove that model (3) has zero conditional mean or that all relevant controls have been included. The model (3) slope \(t\) statistics for zero null values are about \(-206.11\), \(-119.99\), and \(22.90\) for price, income, and gasoline. Each is far from zero relative to its conventional standard error, so all three would be significant at ordinary levels under the maintained inference assumptions. Statistical significance still does not establish causal identification or economic importance in unspecified units. Seminar 1, PDF p. 2, Problem 1(vii); Lecture 1, PDF p. 26

Origin: reused complete checked passage Goodness of fit: R-squared and adjusted R-squared; fingerprint 8cb7c6b76f548352c216ae9bd1d909a788d8d8f5b8718c2721d23989ce332d7f. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Goodness of fit: R-squared and adjusted R-squared

Problem 2 asks for both measures. Worked explanation: with an intercept, define total sum of squares \(\mathrm{SST}=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2\) and residual sum of squares \(\mathrm{SSE}=\sum_i\hat u_i^2\). The latter notation explicitly means residual, rather than explained, sum of squares here. OLS orthogonality gives the decomposition into fitted variation around the mean and residual variation. Therefore

\[R^2=1-\frac{\mathrm{SSE}}{\mathrm{SST}}.\]

For model (3), \(\mathrm{SSE}=94{,}171.050600\) and \(\mathrm{SST}=11{,}096{,}411.524222\), so \(R^2=0.991513\). The fitted model accounts for approximately 99.1513% of the sample variation in travel around its mean. This is a description of sample fit; it is not a statement that the included variables causally explain that share, nor a guarantee of performance on new data. Seminar 1, PDF p. 2, Problem 2; Computed from travel.csv

Adding regressors to the same OLS sample cannot increase the minimized \(SSE\): the original model remains available by setting each new coefficient to zero. Thus \(R^2\) cannot decrease merely because more regressors were allowed. Adjusted \(R^2\) accounts for residual degrees of freedom:

\[\bar R^2 =1-\frac{\mathrm{SSE}/(n-k-1)}{\mathrm{SST}/(n-1)} =1-(1-R^2)\frac{n-1}{n-k-1},\]

where \(k\) counts nonconstant regressors. It can fall if the reduction in \(SSE\) is too small to compensate for the additional parameters, and can be negative for a poorly fitting model. Comparisons should use the same dependent variable and observations. Here both fit measures rise across the three specifications, but that alone cannot determine whether a coefficient has a causal interpretation. For the ten-city regression, \(R^2=0.340477\) and adjusted \(R^2=0.258037\); these are separate results from a separate dataset. Seminar 1, PDF p. 2, Problem 2

A report should state the research question, define variables and known units, justify the specification, describe the observations, show a readable regression table, interpret coefficient magnitudes and uncertainty, explain fit and diagnostic results, and identify the assumptions that remain unsupported. For this exercise, the numerical contrast between simple and multiple regression is central: the estimated price association changes when income is held fixed. The important limitation is equally central: no documented sampling process, structural-error definition, or unit dictionary is supplied for the CSV. The exercise develops empirical reasoning, while the source leaves those provenance details unspecified. sections.title: Prerequisites and checks

sections.html: Dates encode order and lags; they are not interchangeable sampled labels. The whole design \(X\) contains every sample-date regressor and an intercept. Rank \(k+1\) makes the OLS inverse meaningful. Strict exogeneity conditions the date \(t\) error mean on all of \(X\), including future values. Same-date \(E[u_{t}\mid x_{t}]=0\) omits potential feedback: an unexpected outcome today may alter policy/resources tomorrow. Conditional on \(X\), the OLS weights \((X'X)^{-1}X'\) are fixed; therefore \(E[\widehat\beta\mid X]=\beta+A E[u\mid X]=\beta\) when the strict-exogeneity condition makes that full mean vector zero. Then iterate expectation for unconditional unbiasedness. Constant variance, serial covariance and normality enter different results later, not this cancellation. Zero conditional mean implies appropriate zero covariances with finite moments but the converse is not automatic. Failure removes a guarantee, not a proof of universal bias. Suitable weaker conditions may give consistency in contextual Chapter11 passages, without finite-sample unbiasedness; a full next-week theorem is outside these notes. Names/formulas avoid the deck/textbook rank/exogeneity numbering swap.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Temporal ordering and a stochastic process; fingerprint b15a3499dc1e95b326b898a39f5d58f9d72de24432544877ddd9d5a586775e4b. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Temporal ordering and a stochastic process

For cross-sectional observations, the index \(i=1,\ldots,n\) distinguishes sampled units. For a time series, \(t=1,\ldots,T\) distinguishes ordered periods. The model \(y_t=\beta_0+\beta_1x_t+u_t\) looks like its cross-sectional counterpart, but rearranging the dates changes the meaning of lags and dynamics. The lecture treats the observed sequence as one realization of a stochastic process, a collection of random variables indexed by time. Random does not mean independently sampled: an unpredictable sequence can still have dependence across dates. The independence available under the cross-sectional random-sampling assumption is therefore not assumed here. Lecture 2, PDF pp. 4–7

The display \(u_t\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\) on p. 4 describes a marginal distribution, not a complete joint distribution over time. By itself it does not establish that disturbances at different dates are independent or that they are independent of regressors. The later TS assumptions state these restrictions separately. This is an agent clarification of the contrast between the opening model and pp. 11, 16, and 19. Lecture 2, PDF p. 4; Lecture 2, PDF pp. 16–19

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage The first three assumptions; fingerprint b15a3499dc1e95b326b898a39f5d58f9d72de24432544877ddd9d5a586775e4b. Heading depth alone is adapted.

The first three assumptions

Use the numbering in this lecture, which differs from both the Week 1 MLR list and the supplied textbook. In particular, TS2 is strict exogeneity and TS3 is no perfect collinearity. Let \(x_t=(x_{t1},\ldots,x_{tk})\) collect the \(k\) nonconstant regressors at date \(t\), and let \(X\) contain their values at every sample date plus an intercept column. Lecture 2, PDF pp. 10–12

Assumption Formal statement and meaning
TS1: linear in parameters \(y_t=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^k\beta_jx_{tj}+u_t\). Equivalently, \(y=X\beta+u\), where \(y,u\) are \(T\times1\), \(X\) is \(T\times(k+1)\), and \(\beta\) is \((k+1)\times1\).
TS2: zero conditional mean / strict exogeneity \(E[u_t\mid X]=0\) for every \(t\). The mean of the date-\(t\) disturbance is zero conditional on the entire regressor history in the sample, including future dates.
TS3: no perfect collinearity \(\operatorname{rank}(X)=k+1\). No nonconstant regressor is constant or an exact linear combination of the other columns; the intercept itself is intentionally constant. This makes \(X'X\) invertible.

The textbook reverses the deck's TS2/TS3 labels: book TS.2 is no perfect collinearity, book TS.3 is strict exogeneity. Names and formulas therefore matter more than bare numbers. The remaining assumption names correspond. Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 378 (printed p. 350)

These statements unpack the displayed equations and rank condition; \(T\) is used consistently for sample length even where the slides alternate \(n\) and \(T\). There is no replacement assumption that observations themselves are independent. Strict exogeneity restricts regressor–disturbance relationships; it does not rule out all temporal dependence in \(x_t\) or \(y_t\). Lecture 2, PDF pp. 10–13

Strict versus contemporaneous exogeneity

Contemporaneous exogeneity requires only

\[E[u_t\mid x_t]=0.\]

It conditions on the regressors at the same date. TS2 instead requires \(E[u_t\mid x_1,\ldots,x_T]=0\). With finite relevant moments, TS2 implies that \(u_t\) has zero covariance with each included regressor at every sample date \(s\), including \(s\ne t\). It is stronger than those covariance restrictions: zero conditional mean is not merely a statement about linear correlation. Contemporaneous zero conditional mean gives no comparable guarantee about past or future regressors. Lecture 2, PDF pp. 9–11

Under independent cross-sectional sampling, an observation's disturbance and regressors are independent of the other sampled observations. This lets \(E[u_i\mid x_i]=0\) imply \(E[u_i\mid X]=0\). A time series has no such sampling guarantee: an unexpected shock today may help determine a regressor tomorrow. The lecture therefore imposes the full-design condition explicitly. Lecture 2, PDF p. 9

The textbook gives an economic feedback example: a city's murder-rate disturbance can influence how many police officers it hires in the following year. Even if current police numbers are uncorrelated with the current disturbance, future police numbers can react to today's unexpected murder-rate change, violating strict exogeneity. Adding past explanatory variables does not automatically remove feedback to future values. This explains why policy variables chosen in response to past outcomes need particular scrutiny. Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 379 (printed p. 351); Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 380 (printed p. 352)

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Why strict exogeneity gives unbiasedness; fingerprint b15a3499dc1e95b326b898a39f5d58f9d72de24432544877ddd9d5a586775e4b. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Why strict exogeneity gives unbiasedness

Under TS1 and TS3, OLS satisfies

\[\hat\beta=(X'X)^{-1}X'y =\beta+(X'X)^{-1}X'u.\]

Conditional on \(X\), the matrix multiplying \(u\) is fixed. Taking conditional expectation and applying TS2 gives

\[E[\hat\beta\mid X] =\beta+(X'X)^{-1}X'E[u\mid X] =\beta.\]

Taking expectation again yields \(E[\hat\beta]=\beta\), when the relevant expectations exist. This is an agent matrix expansion of the source's scalar proof and matrix theorem. For simple regression its error term is \(\sum_t(x_t-\bar x)u_t/\sum_t(x_t-\bar x)^2\); every weight is fixed only after conditioning on all of \(X\), which is exactly why same-date exogeneity is insufficient for this proof. Lecture 2, PDF pp. 8–13

TS1–TS3 establish finite-sample conditional unbiasedness without homoskedasticity, no serial correlation, or normality. The lecture warns that failing strict exogeneity can produce bias even with contemporaneous exogeneity. Read this as loss of the unbiasedness guarantee: failure of a sufficient condition does not logically prove that every coefficient in every special design is biased. Nor does failure of this finite-sample result settle consistency; the lecture assigns large-sample issues to the next week. Lecture 2, PDF pp. 11, 13, 31

Steps and interpretation: \(y,u\) are \(20\times 1\), \(X\) is \(20\times 3\), \(\beta\) is \(3\times 1\); \(\operatorname{rank}(X)=3\) gives invertible \(X^{\top}X\). A process is a time-indexed collection of random variables; this sequence is one realisation, not independent random sampling. Strict exogeneity is \(E[u_t\mid X\text{ at all sample dates}]=0\); the stated feedback to future regressors means same-date condition alone is insufficient and the full condition may fail. Without full \(E[u\mid X]=0\) that cancellation is not justified. Consistency is a separate large-sample property needing suitable dependence/exogeneity/rank conditions; the notes provide only bounded next-week context.
