sections.title: Prerequisites and checks

sections.html: Set \(A=(X'X)^{-1}X'\). With whole \(X\) fixed, \(\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta\mid X)=A\Omega A\prime\) where \(\Omega=\operatorname{Var}(u\mid X)\). Homoskedasticity controls diagonals, no serial correlation controls off-diagonals; together \(\Omega=\sigma^2 I\) and \(A\Omega A'=\sigma^2(X'X)^{-1}\). In simple regression the slope is a weighted error sum, whose variance contains both \(\sum_t a_t^2\sigma_t^2\) and \(2\sum_{t<s}a_ta_s\operatorname{Cov}(u_t,u_s\mid X)\) terms. Dropping cross terms requires the covariance assumption. Multiple-regression precision depends on regressor variation left after the others: \(SST_j(1-R_j^2)\), with an auxiliary—not outcome—\(R^2\). Estimate \(\sigma^2\) by \(SSR/(T-k-1)\); all coefficients including intercept consume degrees of freedom. These assumptions make OLS BLUE conditional on \(X\) among linear unbiased estimators. Exact null \(t\) and joint \(F\) require additionally errors independent of \(X\) and iid normal, not merely normal marginals. Normal errors imply the named mean/variance/no-serial conditions, but never rank. Serial correlation can coexist with strict exogeneity/unbiasedness while invalidating the simplified variance and exact-inference use. Alternative covariance estimators are future content, not improvised here.
sections.title: Motivation and explanation

sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Two additional assumptions for conventional variance; fingerprint b15a3499dc1e95b326b898a39f5d58f9d72de24432544877ddd9d5a586775e4b. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Two additional assumptions for conventional variance

TS4 requires \(\operatorname{Var}(u_t\mid X)=\sigma^2\) for each date: the conditional variance is constant over time and does not depend on any sample-date regressors. TS5 requires \(\operatorname{Cov}(u_t,u_s\mid X)=0\) for \(t\ne s\); the slide writes the equivalent zero-correlation condition when variances are positive. Nonzero covariance across dates is serial correlation, also called autocorrelation. These are different restrictions: constant variance does not make cross-date covariances zero. Lecture 2, PDF pp. 15–17

Together they give the \(T\times T\) covariance matrix

\[\operatorname{Var}(u\mid X)=\sigma^2 I_T.\]

Every diagonal element is the same variance and every off-diagonal element is zero. The lower matrix on source p. 17 omits the conditioning symbol; the text and upper equation explicitly condition on \(X\), which is the interpretation used here. Under TS2 and constant conditional variance, the law of total variance also gives \(\operatorname{Var}(u_t)=\sigma^2\), explaining the unconditional equality printed on p. 15. Lecture 2, PDF pp. 15, 17

Source crop: Lecture 2, PDF p. 17. Equal diagonal entries express homoskedasticity; zero off-diagonal entries express no conditional serial correlation. The matrix concerns disturbances, not an assertion that regressors at different dates are uncorrelated. Source, PDF p. 17

The covariance terms hidden in the simple-slope proof

Define \(S_{xx}=\sum_t(x_t-\bar x)^2\) and \(a_t=(x_t-\bar x)/S_{xx}\). Conditional on \(X\), the slope error is \(\sum_t a_tu_t\). Expanding its variance gives

\[\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1\mid X) =\sum_t a_t^2\operatorname{Var}(u_t\mid X) +2\sum_{t<s}a_ta_s\operatorname{Cov}(u_t,u_s\mid X).\]

TS5 removes the second sum. TS4 then replaces each variance by \(\sigma^2\), leaving

\[\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1\mid X) =\frac{\sigma^2\sum_t(x_t-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}^2} =\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}.\]

This expansion supplies the intermediate justification requested by p. 14. More regressor variation reduces slope uncertainty under these conditions. Serial correlation need not destroy unbiasedness under TS1–TS3, but its covariance terms invalidate this simplified variance formula. Lecture 2, PDF pp. 14–18

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Multiple-regression precision, residual variance, and BLUE; fingerprint b15a3499dc1e95b326b898a39f5d58f9d72de24432544877ddd9d5a586775e4b. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Multiple-regression precision, residual variance, and BLUE

Under TS1–TS5,

\[\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta\mid X)=\sigma^2(X'X)^{-1}, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_j\mid X)= \frac{\sigma^2}{SST_j(1-R_j^2)},\quad j=1,\ldots,k.\]

Here \(SST_j=\sum_t(x_{tj}-\bar x_j)^2\). The auxiliary-regression \(R_j^2\) comes from regressing regressor \(j\) on an intercept and the other explanatory variables; it is not the \(R^2\) of the original outcome regression. The product \(SST_j(1-R_j^2)\) is variation in regressor \(j\) left after the other regressors explain it. When that independent variation is small, separating coefficient \(j\) is imprecise. Perfect collinearity makes it zero and violates TS3; substantial but imperfect correlation raises variance without itself creating bias. The matrix formula is an agent derivation from the source's covariance matrix and scalar theorem. Lecture 2, PDF pp. 17–18

Let \(\hat u_t=y_t-\hat y_t\) and define the residual sum of squares \(SSR=\sum_t\hat u_t^2\). The source uses \(SSR\) for this residual quantity. With \(k\) nonconstant regressors plus an intercept,

\[\hat\sigma^2=\frac{SSR}{T-k-1}\]

is unbiased for \(\sigma^2\) under TS1–TS5. The denominator is residual degrees of freedom, not \(T\), because \(k+1\) coefficients have been estimated. Substituting \(\hat\sigma^2\) in the coefficient variance formula and taking its square root gives the conventional estimated standard error. These variance estimates require the assumptions used in deriving them; a regression program printing a standard error does not verify those assumptions. Lecture 2, PDF p. 18, Theorems 2–3

The same assumptions yield the time-series Gauss–Markov theorem: OLS is best linear unbiased conditional on \(X\). Linear means linear in the observed outcomes with weights determined by \(X\); best means smallest conditional variance in the linear-unbiased comparison class. It is not a comparison with every possible biased or nonlinear estimator. Lecture 2, PDF p. 18, Theorem 4

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Normality and exact finite-sample inference; fingerprint b15a3499dc1e95b326b898a39f5d58f9d72de24432544877ddd9d5a586775e4b. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Normality and exact finite-sample inference

TS6 states that disturbances are independent of \(X\) and independently and identically distributed as \(N(0,\sigma^2)\). Together with linearity and full rank this makes \(\hat\beta\mid X\) normal. The source's full TS1–TS6 list yields exact null \(t\) and \(F\) distributions. For one coefficient and null value \(\beta_{j,0}\),

\[t_j=\frac{\hat\beta_j-\beta_{j,0}}{\operatorname{se}(\hat\beta_j)} \sim t_{T-k-1}\quad\text{under }H_0.\]

Joint tests compare multiple restrictions using an \(F\) statistic. The displayed \(t\) formula and degrees of freedom are an agent expansion of Theorem 5, using the residual degrees of freedom supplied on p. 18. Normality adds an exact-distribution conclusion; it was not required for the preceding unbiasedness or BLUE results. Lecture 2, PDF pp. 18–20

Source numbering error. Page 19 says “TS6 implies TS3–TS5.” In this deck TS3 is full rank (p. 12), which cannot follow from a distributional assumption on disturbances: two identical regressor columns remain identical even with independent normal errors. TS6 does imply the source's zero-conditional-mean, constant-variance, and no-serial-correlation conditions (TS2, TS4, TS5), but TS3 must be checked separately. The supplied textbook resolves the origin of this discrepancy: its corresponding statement is correct because book TS.3 is strict exogeneity, while the deck assigned that name to TS2. Thus the implication survives by name, but the deck's copied number range does not. Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 383 (printed p. 355) Lecture 2, PDF p. 19, last line; TS3 definition, PDF p. 12

Chapter 11 clarifies the boundary without changing the Week 2 theorem: with the book's suitable weak-dependence, linear-model and full-rank conditions, contemporaneous exogeneity can yield consistency without finite-sample unbiasedness. Weak dependence means sufficiently limited dependence at widely separated dates for the relevant limit arguments. This is contextual support for why the next lecture relaxes strict exogeneity, not a complete treatment of next-week asymptotic theory. Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 412 (printed p. 384); Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 413 (printed p. 385); Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 414 (printed p. 386)

What the assumption ladder establishes

TS1–TS3 provide a conditional-unbiasedness guarantee. TS4–TS5 justify conventional variances, unbiased residual-variance estimation, and conditional BLUE. TS6 supplies exact finite-sample normal and null-test distributions. Strict exogeneity and no serial correlation are restrictive in many social-science time series; the lecture does not claim they hold automatically. Its next-week preparation is Chapter 11 and revision of expected value, variance, covariance, and large-sample OLS properties. The supplied Fifth Edition places Chapter 10 at printed pp. 344–379 (PDF pp. 372–407) and Chapter 11 at printed pp. 380–411 (PDF pp. 408–439), rather than the different-edition page ranges on slide p. 2. Chapter 10 supports these same explanations. Chapter 11 remains next-week reading; only passages directly needed to clarify the current assumption boundary were used, and the linked video was not opened. Lecture 2, PDF pp. 21, 31

O010-W1 / item_version 1, worked_example. Prompt: Hypothetical full-rank time-series linear model with strict exogeneity: \(T=20, k=2\) slopes plus intercept, \(SSR=34\), regressor \(SST_j=10\), auxiliary \(R_j^2=0.5\); \(\hat\beta_j=1.2\), null \(\beta_j=0\). Explain separately the conditional error covariance assumptions needed for conventional variance, derive the matrix and scalar formulas (show the simple-slope covariance sum), calculate \(\hat\sigma^2\) and illustrative plug-in coefficient variance, and the conventional \(\mathrm{SE}, t\) and null degrees of freedom from that same estimated variance. State the exact BLUE comparison class, what stronger error condition makes \(t\) and \(F\) exact, and what fails if serial covariance is nonzero or only marginal normality is known. Can normality restore identical regressor columns?

Steps and interpretation: Homoskedastic \(\operatorname{Var}(u_t\mid X)=\sigma^2\) and no serial \(\operatorname{Cov}(u_t,u_s\mid X)=0\) give \(\Omega=\sigma^2 I_T\); they are separate restrictions. For weights \(a_t=(x_t-\bar x)/S_{xx}\), \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1\mid X)=\sum_t a_t^2\operatorname{Var}(u_t\mid X)+2\sum_{t<s}a_ta_s\operatorname{Cov}(u_t,u_s\mid X)\); zero covariances then constant variance yield \(\sigma^2/S_{xx}\). Matrix \(A\Omega A'=\sigma^2(X'X)^{-1}\), scalar \(\sigma^2/[SST_j(1-R_j^2)]\). \(\mathrm{df}=20-2-1=17\); \(\hat\sigma^2=34/17=2.000000\); illustrative coefficient \(\text{variance}=2.000000/[10\times (1-0.5)]=0.400000\). Conventional \(\mathrm{SE}=\sqrt{0.400000}=0.632456\); requested \(t=(1.2-0)/0.632456=1.897367\), exact null \(t_{\mathrm{df}=17}\) only under full linear/rank/exogeneity plus errors independent of \(X\) and iid \(N(0,\sigma^2)\); joint classical null \(F\) also needs those conditions. BLUE is minimum conditional variance among estimators linear in \(y\) and conditionally unbiased, not all estimators. Serial covariance leaves cross terms: unbiasedness can survive strict exogeneity but conventional variance/SE/exact tests are not justified by these formulas. Marginal \(N(0,\sigma^2)\) alone establishes neither independence across dates nor from \(X\). Error normality never restores full rank; exact duplicate regressor columns still make \(X^{\top}X\) singular. Auxiliary \(R^2\) is from regressing \(x_{j}\) on other regressors, not outcome goodness-of-fit.

sections.title: Prerequisites and checks

sections.html: An FDL of order \(q\) contains current \(z\) and \(q\) lags, with \(q+1\) slopes. Compare paths holding disturbances/other regressors fixed. A pulse at one date changes just one slot in each future equation: \(\delta_h\) for \(0\le h\le q\), then \(0\). A maintained step progressively fills all slots, giving \(\sum_{j=0}^{\min(h,q)}\delta_j\); its eventual level difference is the LRP sum. Units inherit the outcome/regressor transformation. Without prior history \(q\) first rows cannot construct lags. Static means remove lagged slopes, not current \(\delta_0\). For \(q=2\) set \(\theta=\delta_0+\delta_1+\delta_2\) and substitute \(\delta_0=\theta-\delta_1-\delta_2\): \(\theta\) multiplies \(z_{t}\) while \(\delta_1\)/\(\delta_2\) multiply lag-minus-current contrasts. Equivalent columns let the software report the \(\mathrm{SE}\) of \(\theta\) directly. Alternatively \(\operatorname{Var}(\sum_j\widehat\delta_j)=\sum_j\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\delta_j)+2\sum_{j<k}\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat\delta_j,\widehat\delta_k)\). Separate SEs alone omit covariance. Correlated lags may hurt individual precision without proving that the sum is imprecise. Model paths, source intervention examples and timing plots are not causal estimates; unprovided data/coding and unverified policy dates remain boundaries.

Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Static and finite distributed lag models; fingerprint 9e8cb8c0eeff46c0f43ff601c85d5abac60a13edb674569501974f4f61867849. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Static and finite distributed lag models

Does a change in an explanatory variable affect the outcome immediately, over several later periods, or both? A static time-series model represents a contemporaneous relationship. A finite distributed lag (FDL) model lets the adjustment unfold over a specified number of periods. Distinguishing a temporary pulse from a permanent change is essential: a coefficient describes the response at one lag, while a sum of coefficients describes the eventual response to a maintained change. Lecture 2, PDF pp. 22–24

Back to Econometrics II — Week 2. These specifications can be estimated by OLS, but Time-series OLS and strict exogeneity (strict exogeneity and unbiasedness; variance and exact inference) explains the assumptions needed for unbiasedness and inference. Model coefficients are not automatically causal effects.

A static contemporaneous model

The lecture's static specification is

\[y_t=\beta_0+\beta_1z_t+u_t,\qquad t=1,\ldots,T.\]

Here \(z_t\) is the explanatory variable at the same date as outcome \(y_t\), and \(u_t\) collects other influences. The coefficients are time-invariant. Holding the disturbance unchanged, a change in \(z\) gives \(\Delta y_t=\beta_1\Delta z_t\); the contemporaneous slope has units of outcome per unit of \(z\). This is the source's comparison with \(\Delta u_t=0\). It does not say that real observed outcomes change only because of \(z\), or that disturbances necessarily stay fixed between successive calendar dates. Lecture 2, PDF p. 22

The source's demand example is \(D_t=\beta_0+\beta_1Price_t+u_t\), a same-period tradeoff between consumption and price. The specification assumes that the intercept and slope do not change over time. Whether price is exogenous is an additional question: writing a demand equation does not establish that price changes independently of unobserved demand influences. This qualification connects the example to the source's TS2 requirement. Lecture 2, PDF p. 22; Strict exogeneity, PDF p. 11

An FDL model spreads adjustment across dates

For lag order \(q\), write

\[y_t=\alpha_0+\delta_0z_t+\delta_1z_{t-1}+\cdots+\delta_qz_{t-q}+u_t.\]

The lagged variable \(z_{t-j}\) is the value \(j\) periods earlier. There are \(q\) lagged values plus the current value, so an FDL of order two has three slope coefficients. Each \(\delta_j\) has units of \(y\) per unit of \(z\) and describes the model's date-\(t\) response to a change in the value of \(z\) at date \(t-j\), holding the other included values and disturbances fixed. The period is set by data frequency: one lag in monthly data means one month. Lecture 2, PDF pp. 23, 25

Wooldridge likewise treats the static model as current-value-only and the FDL as a current value plus a finite set of earlier values. Its fertility example makes the lag rationale explicit: biological and behavioral decisions can delay the response of births to the tax value of a child. Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 374 (printed p. 346)

Constructing lags requires earlier observations. If the available raw series begins at date 1 and no earlier \(z\) is supplied, a model with \(q\) lags can first use date \(q+1\). Its estimation sample length is the number of usable rows, not automatically the original series length. This is an agent bookkeeping implication of the displayed indices, relevant when using \(T-k-1\) degrees of freedom from the OLS note. Lecture 2, PDF p. 23; Residual degrees of freedom, PDF p. 18

A temporary pulse and a permanent step

Agent derivation of the source's response interpretation. Compare two regressor paths that share the same disturbance path and all other model inputs. With a one-unit temporary pulse at date \(s\), \(\Delta z_s=1\) and \(\Delta z_t=0\) at all other dates. Substituting in the FDL gives

\[\Delta y_{s+h}=\delta_h\quad(0\le h\le q), \qquad \Delta y_{s+h}=0\quad(h>q).\]

The impact propensity is \(\delta_0\), the immediate response. The date-\(s+1\) response is \(\delta_1\), and so on. From \(q+1\) periods onward the pulse has left every included regressor position, so it has no further response in this finite-lag specification. This conclusion is a model implication, not a guarantee about an economic system whose effects might last longer than the chosen lag order. Lecture 2, PDF p. 23, temporary increase

For a permanent one-unit increase starting at \(s\), \(\Delta z_t=1\) for every \(t\ge s\). At the first date only the current regressor has changed. One period later both the current and first-lag regressor have changed. Continuing this substitution gives

\[\Delta y_{s+h}=\sum_{j=0}^{\min(h,q)}\delta_j, \qquad LRP=\sum_{j=0}^{q}\delta_j.\]

The long-run propensity (LRP) is the final level difference once all included lags carry the maintained change. It is not the effect in the first period, nor an estimate of a percentage change unless the model's units or transformations justify that interpretation. Lecture 2, PDF p. 23, permanent increase

For order two, the contrast is:

Period relative to change Temporary one-unit pulse Permanent one-unit increase
\(s\) \(\delta_0\) \(\delta_0\)
\(s+1\) \(\delta_1\) \(\delta_0+\delta_1\)
\(s+2\) \(\delta_2\) \(\delta_0+\delta_1+\delta_2\)
\(s+3\) and later \(0\) \(\delta_0+\delta_1+\delta_2\)

Agent-created table derived from the order-two equation and temporary/permanent comparisons on Lecture 2, PDF p. 23. For example, hypothetical coefficients \((2,0.5,-0.5)\) give pulse responses \((2,0.5,-0.5,0,\ldots)\) and step responses \((2,2.5,2,2,\ldots)\). A negative later response can offset part of an initial increase, so a large impact propensity does not require an equally large long-run propensity. These numbers are an illustration, not an estimated course result. Source model, PDF p. 23

Source Figure 10.1: an illustrative lag distribution, with the largest pulse response at lag 1 and a zero response after lag 2. The horizontal axis is lag, and the vertical axis is a coefficient, not a measured outcome series. The diagram is schematic and contains no numerical coefficient estimates. Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 375 (printed p. 347)

The textbook's explicit substitutions for a temporary pulse and maintained step give the same response sequences as the table above. Whether an economic response really ends after the chosen number of lags remains an empirical specification question. Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 375 (printed p. 347); Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 376 (printed p. 348)

A static model is a special case, with a source caveat

Setting only the lag coefficients \(\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_q\) to zero leaves \(y_t=\alpha_0+\delta_0z_t+u_t\), the static model. The arrows on p. 24 show zeros under the lagged terms. Its accompanying text, however, says to set \(\delta_0,\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_q\) to zero. Taken literally, that also removes the contemporaneous regressor and leaves an intercept-only model. The static-model definition on p. 22 and the p. 24 arrows support retaining \(\delta_0\); the inconsistent source wording is explicitly recorded here. Wooldridge states the special case unambiguously by setting \(\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_q\) to zero while retaining the current-value coefficient. Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 376 (printed p. 348) Lecture 2, PDF p. 24; Static definition, PDF p. 22

Values of \(z\) at nearby dates are often strongly correlated. This can make the individual \(\delta_j\) estimates imprecise, because there is little independent variation to distinguish their contributions. Substantial lag correlation is imperfect multicollinearity; exact dependence violates full rank. The distinction follows the multiple-regression variance denominator \(SST_j(1-R_j^2)\) in the OLS note. Adding lags is therefore an economic modeling choice with a precision cost, not a mechanical way to improve identification. Lecture 2, PDF p. 24, lag correlation; Variance theorem, PDF p. 18

Precision of the long-run sum

Imprecise individual lag estimates do not imply that their sum is equally imprecise. In the textbook's annual fertility illustration (United States, 1913–1984; 70 usable rows after two lags), the coefficients on current and lagged real personal-exemption values are approximately \(0.073\), \(-0.0058\), and \(0.034\). Their individual standard errors are large, but their estimated sum is about \(0.101\) births per 1,000 women of childbearing age per dollar, with standard error \(0.030\). The source reports a 95% interval of approximately \(0.041\) to \(0.160\), conditional on its maintained model. This is a textbook result, not a recomputed result from a supplied dataset. Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 386 (printed p. 358); Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 387 (printed p. 359)

To see why separate standard errors are insufficient, an agent expansion of the variance-of-a-sum identity gives

\[\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{LRP}\mid X) =\sum_{j=0}^q\operatorname{Var}(\hat\delta_j\mid X) +2\sum_{j<\ell}\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\delta_j,\hat\delta_\ell\mid X).\]

The coefficient covariances are needed. The book obtains the sum's standard error by reparameterizing an order-two model with \(\theta=\delta_0+\delta_1+\delta_2\):

\[y_t=\alpha_0+\theta z_t +\delta_1(z_{t-1}-z_t)+\delta_2(z_{t-2}-z_t)+u_t.\]

This follows by substituting \(\delta_0=\theta-\delta_1-\delta_2\). A regression on these transformed columns estimates the same model, with the coefficient on \(z_t\) directly equal to the LRP and its reported standard error attached to that sum. Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 386 (printed p. 358); Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 387 (printed p. 359)

The EET restaurant-price example

The lecture asks whether electronic sales reporting (EET), introduced to reduce tax evasion, affects restaurant prices. It proposes monthly restaurant-price-index data from the Czech Statistical Office and a four-lag model:

\[priceindex_t=\alpha_0+\delta_0EET_t+\delta_1EET_{t-1} +\delta_2EET_{t-2}+\delta_3EET_{t-3}+\delta_4EET_{t-4}+u_t.\]

The source gives no dataset, coefficient estimates, exact variable coding, or identification design. Conditional coding explanation: if \(EET_t\) is a zero/one indicator for an active regime, a maintained switch from zero to one has immediate model difference \(\delta_0\) and final difference \(\delta_0+\cdots+\delta_4\), in price-index points. Other influences on prices remain in \(u_t\), so this response becomes a causal policy effect only with a defensible exogeneity/specification argument. A fitted intervention model alone cannot establish that argument. Lecture 2, PDF p. 25; Exogeneity requirement, PDF p. 11

A price index needs a base period and base value: an index-point change is different from a percentage change or a currency-unit change. For positive index values, the percentage change from date \(a\) to \(b\) is \(100(I_b/I_a-1)\). The slide does not specify the restaurant index's base. This brief index clarification is supplied by the textbook and prevents treating the displayed coefficient as a price change in crowns or as a percentage by default. Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 388 (printed p. 360)

Source-context boundary: p. 25 states introduction in December 2016, cancellation on January 1, 2023, and reintroduction on January 1, 2027. These are the lecture's policy-context statements; their current legal/calendar accuracy was not independently verified against an authorized external source. They must not be used as confirmed current policy facts. The econometric exercise does not require accepting the claimed future date. No external media or statistical-office link was opened during this ingestion. Lecture 2, PDF p. 25, opening paragraph

A visual motivation for lagged response

Original embedded image from Lecture 2, PDF p. 35. Upper panel: daily newly confirmed COVID-19 cases per million people in Czechia; lower panel: the number of patients in hospital. Both cover dates in early 2022. The upper panel explicitly warns that limited testing means confirmed cases undercount infections; the original source/credit text is preserved. Lecture 2, PDF p. 35

The source places these plots under “Lagged effects.” The waves appear at different stages, motivating a model in which an explanatory series can precede an outcome response. The units differ, and hospital occupancy is not a count of newly admitted patients; comparing peak heights is therefore not a response coefficient. The image supplies neither an estimated lag length nor an FDL fit, and its timing alone does not identify causation. It illustrates why immediate-only specifications may miss dynamics. Lecture 2, PDF p. 35, both panels

What to retain

A static model contains the current explanatory variable; an FDL additionally contains its lags. Read \(\delta_j\) as the date-\(j\) response to a temporary unit pulse, and read their sum as the final response to a permanent unit step, under the model and held-fixed disturbance comparison. Strong correlation between lags affects precision; assumptions about disturbances determine whether these modeled comparisons support unbiased or causal interpretation. Lecture 2, PDF pp. 23–25

sections.html:
Self-assessment criteria and tutor checks

Pass requires every listed component, all requested outputs and essential keyed reasoning without a critical conceptual error. Algebraically equivalent formulas, explicitly defined opposite cash-flow signs and equivalent plain-language reasoning are accepted. Partial means a missing component or a correct method with an unresolved isolated arithmetic slip; fail means the central mechanism or condition is wrong. Unscorable means the response or help/exposure conditions cannot be established. Unknown conditions never certify independence. Arithmetic slips require independent correction before a pass. No numerical grade is invented.

Critical errors: Using LRP for a temporary pulse each period; adding \(q+1\) lost rows; static deletes \(\delta_0\); summing standard errors; index points called percent causal effects without conditions.

Acquisition requires two distinct unassisted passes from I1/I2/D1/D2 using the exact six routes in metadata. Each full prompt and key covers every component; any pair therefore covers the whole outcome twice. A fresh D item used for acquisition cannot later certify delayed retention. Worked/support/prerequisite items and the narrow C1 correction cannot substitute for a full check. The finite bank must not be reused after exposure; request a plan_issue when fewer than two fresh full items remain.

sections.title: Prerequisites and checks

sections.html: A deterministic linear trend shifts expected levels by units per period; a linear log trend on positive outcomes models approximately \(100b_1\%\) growth; a quadratic permits curvature. These time forms are substantive choices, not arbitrary polynomial tracking. If the true comparison includes \(\gamma t\) but the regression omits it, \(u_t=\gamma t+\varepsilon_t\) may be correlated with trending \(x\). Include the relevant controls or residualise \(y\) and every substantive \(x\) on exactly the same intercept/time basis and rows. In the full regression, \(e\) is orthogonal to \(1,t,x\). Since \(x_t=a_x+b_xt+\tilde x_t\) and the residualised columns are orthogonal to \(1,t\), \(\sum_t\tilde x_t e_t=0\); summing their equation yields \(\widehat\beta=\sum_t\tilde x_t\tilde y_t/\sum_t\tilde x_t^2\) when denominator \(>0\). It is a sample identity, not exogeneity. \(SSR\) is the same, but detrended \(R^2\) divides by \(\sum_t\tilde y_t^2\); full \(R^2\) divides by original \(TSS\). A strong time fit can coexist with weak residual \(x\) fit, as in the noted housing example. Full model degrees of freedom remain \(T-3\) for intercept/trend/one \(x\). Exact \(x\) trend causes rank failure; perfectly trend-fitted \(y\) makes residual \(R^2\) undefined. Correctly specified deterministic controls address that component, not every persistent process, serial correlation or causal identification.
sections.title: Motivation and explanation

sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage What the source's three trend plots show; fingerprint 0e7fb5c1af7cabc4ea80572915d3578a657db087254f5d6e70a4f870eabc185f. Heading depth alone is adapted.

What the source's three trend plots show

Original embedded image: GDP against productivity, Lecture 2, PDF p. 32. The connected observations show a strong positive association in levels; the axes provide variable names and numeric scales but no units or country/sample provenance. Lecture 2, PDF p. 32

Original embedded image: GDP against Year, Lecture 2, PDF p. 33. GDP generally increases over the displayed years, with a pause or decline around the late 2000s. Lecture 2, PDF p. 33

Original embedded image: productivity against Year, Lecture 2, PDF p. 34. Productivity also generally increases over the displayed years. Lecture 2, PDF p. 34

Together the plots make the lecture's concern concrete: the positive relationship in the first image is observed between two variables that both trend in time. They do not establish that the entire relationship is spurious, nor do they provide detrended estimates or a causal test. The missing units and dataset provenance prevent a numerical slope interpretation from these figures alone. Their role is to motivate controlling the time pattern rather than treating the raw association as decisive evidence. Lecture 2, PDF pp. 26, 32–34

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Choose a time form that matches the comparison; fingerprint 0e7fb5c1af7cabc4ea80572915d3578a657db087254f5d6e70a4f870eabc185f. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Choose a time form that matches the comparison

A linear trend \(y_t=a_0+a_1t+e_t\) has expected level \(E[y_t]=a_0+a_1t\) when \(E[e_t]=0\); \(a_1\) is an average level change per period. A constant average percentage growth rate instead suggests a linear trend in the logarithm, \(\log y_t=b_0+b_1t+e_t\) for \(y_t>0\), with small-change growth approximately \(100b_1\%\) per period. A quadratic trend adds \(a_2t^2\) to allow curvature. These are alternative representations of a deterministic time pattern, not interchangeable instructions to apply the same linear trend to every original series. Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 392 (printed p. 364); Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 393 (printed p. 365); Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 394 (printed p. 366)

The textbook cautions against adding enough polynomial terms merely to track every movement: a simple broad time pattern serves the substantive model better than an arbitrarily flexible curve. A trend can coexist with correlated deviations around it, so trending variables do not automatically violate the classical assumptions if the model properly includes the relevant pattern. Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 394 (printed p. 366); Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 396 (printed p. 368)

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Shared trends as an omitted-variable problem; fingerprint 0e7fb5c1af7cabc4ea80572915d3578a657db087254f5d6e70a4f870eabc185f. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Shared trends as an omitted-variable problem

The lecture calls a relationship spurious correlation when the apparent association arises simply because both variables grow over time. Its explanation is that trending influences on \(y_t\) are omitted and correlated with an explanatory variable. This can violate zero conditional mean, the condition required by the time-series unbiasedness proof. Lecture 2, PDF pp. 26–27

Agent algebraic illustration of that mechanism. Suppose the intended specification is

\[y_t=\beta_0+\beta_1x_t+\gamma t+\varepsilon_t.\]

If we omit \(t\), the short-model disturbance becomes \(u_t=\gamma t+\varepsilon_t\). If \(x_t\) also trends, its values can be correlated with this omitted component. The short-model slope then absorbs some common time pattern rather than isolating the relationship conditional on time. A large raw \(R^2\) does not demonstrate that the substantive regressor accounts for the movement independently of trend. This example explains the source's omitted-variable interpretation; it is not an estimated equation for its GDP/productivity figures. Lecture 2, PDF pp. 26–28

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Include an appropriate time trend; fingerprint 0e7fb5c1af7cabc4ea80572915d3578a657db087254f5d6e70a4f870eabc185f. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Include an appropriate time trend

The source's first remedy is to include the missing time variable in the regression. In the illustrative linear-trend model above, \(t\) counts periods, \(\gamma\) measures the systematic change per period, and \(\beta_1\) compares \(y\) and \(x\) after holding this time component fixed. The trend is an additional regressor, so it must satisfy the design's full-rank requirement. If \(x\) is exactly a linear function of the intercept and \(t\), its separate slope cannot be identified; if it is nearly so, the coefficient may be imprecise. This is an agent application of TS3 to the source's remedy. Lecture 2, PDF p. 28; Full rank, PDF p. 12

The advantage is a simple single regression. The source warns that its overall \(R^2\) can be high because the trend explains much of the original outcome variation. That \(R^2\) measures the fit of all included regressors, including time; it does not isolate the explanatory contribution of the substantive variable. Page 28 describes the difficulty as being unable to tell what portion is explained by explanatory variables when time is not counted as a substantive explanatory variable. Read this as a warning about interpreting the overall \(R^2\), rather than a statement that no conditional comparison is possible. Lecture 2, PDF p. 28, pros and cons

Qualification of the source's remedy: pp. 28–29 say that adding a trend or detrending eliminates the problem. The appropriate claim is conditional: removing a correctly specified common deterministic trend addresses that omitted component. Merely adding some trend does not prove exogeneity or remove every possible time-series specification problem. The uploaded slides provide no formal result guaranteeing that a linear trend cures arbitrary trending processes. Lecture 2, PDF pp. 28–29

The textbook also distinguishes deterministic trend from strong persistence. Its next-week discussion shows that a process can have a trending mean without strong persistence, or strong persistence without an obvious trend; fitting a deterministic trend is therefore not a universal treatment for all persistent processes. Only this limitation is carried into Week 2; random-walk derivations and transformation methods remain next-week material. Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 422 (printed p. 394); Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 423 (printed p. 395)

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Detrend every variable using the same time form; fingerprint 0e7fb5c1af7cabc4ea80572915d3578a657db087254f5d6e70a4f870eabc185f. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Detrend every variable using the same time form

The second remedy regresses each modeled variable on time and uses the residuals in the substantive regression. Agent expansion of the source's linear-trend procedure: first estimate

\[y_t=a_y+b_yt+\tilde y_t, \qquad x_t=a_x+b_xt+\tilde x_t\]

by OLS over the same sample, including an intercept in both detrending regressions. The residual \(\tilde y_t\) is the outcome's deviation from its fitted time trend, and \(\tilde x_t\) is the corresponding regressor deviation. Then regress \(\tilde y_t\) on \(\tilde x_t\). With multiple substantive regressors, detrend each one against the same intercept/trend columns and sample. The source stresses using the same form of time trend for all variables; changing the form or rows changes what is being removed. Lecture 2, PDF p. 29

Wooldridge explicitly confirms this residualization procedure and its equal-slope interpretation for the same sample and trend controls, including polynomial trends. Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 397 (printed p. 369)

Why the slope agrees with including the trend

The source gives no board-work derivation. The following is an agent derivation from OLS normal equations that makes the proposed method executable. In the full regression of \(y\) on an intercept, \(t\), and \(x\), let \(e_t\) be the fitted residual. It is orthogonal to the intercept and time: \(\sum_te_t=\sum_tte_t=0\). It is also orthogonal to \(x\): \(\sum_tx_te_t=0\). Since \(x_t=a_x+b_xt+\tilde x_t\), these equations imply \(\sum_t\tilde x_te_t=0\).

The detrended variables are themselves orthogonal to the intercept and time. Substituting the two detrending decompositions into the full model and multiplying by \(\tilde x_t\), the intercept/time terms drop out of the summed equation. Therefore

\[\hat\beta_1 =\frac{\sum_t\tilde x_t\tilde y_t} {\sum_t\tilde x_t^2},\]

which is exactly the residual-regression slope, provided the denominator is positive. This shows why detrending both variables with identical controls isolates the same slope as including those controls in the full OLS regression. It does not supply an exogeneity assumption; it is a sample algebraic identity. The reasoning extends to several substantive regressors by their joint normal equations. Lecture 2, PDF p. 29, detrending procedure; OLS normal equations

Because the detrended residuals have zero mean, the residual regression has fitted intercept zero when an intercept is included. Its \(R^2\) can be written as

\[R^2_{detrended}=1-\frac{\sum_t e_t^2}{\sum_t\tilde y_t^2}.\]

The denominator is outcome variation remaining after removal of the fitted trend, not the original outcome's total variation. Its interpretation is the fraction of that remaining variation fitted by the detrended substantive regressors. If \(y\) is perfectly explained by the trend, this denominator is zero and the detrended \(R^2\) is undefined. The source's claim that this \(R^2\) is informative should be read with its changed denominator in view. Lecture 2, PDF p. 29, \(R^2\) interpretation

A concrete textbook example explains why the denominator matters. For 42 annual U.S. housing observations (1947–1988), the estimated log-price elasticity of real per-capita housing investment is \(1.241\) (standard error \(0.382\)) without a trend, but \(-0.381\) (standard error \(0.679\)) with a linear trend. The trend-model overall \(R^2\) is \(0.341\), while the version that first nets the trend out of the outcome has \(R^2=0.008\). The substantive price variable explains very little of the deviations around trend in that fitted model. The book cautions that separate trend-regression standard errors may be unreliable because of serial correlation; these are reported textbook estimates, not independent data re-estimates or proof of no economic price effect. Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 395 (printed p. 367); Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 399 (printed p. 371)

The same source confirms \(1-SSR/\sum_t\tilde y_t^2\) and the need to preserve full-model degrees of freedom. For a classical \(F\) test computed using an \(R^2\) formula, use the usual full/restricted-model \(R^2\) values, not a substitute detrended goodness-of-fit measure. Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 398 (printed p. 370); Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 399 (printed p. 371)

Inference bookkeeping: equal slopes do not license naive degrees of freedom from a second-stage software printout. In the example with an intercept, one time trend, and one substantive regressor, the full model estimates three coefficients, so conventional residual degrees of freedom are \(T-3\). Use the full regression for its standard errors, or preserve the full-model degrees of freedom and assumptions when calculating them from residualized data. This is an agent implication of the p. 18 degrees-of-freedom formula. Lecture 2, PDF p. 18
sections.title: Read the full explanation

sections.html:
O012-W1 / item_version 1, worked_example. Prompt: Hypothetical model includes intercept, linear time and one substantive \(x\), sample \(T=8\). Consistent residualisation on the same rows/time controls gives \(\tilde x=(1,-1,-1,1,0,\ldots,0)\) and \(\tilde y=(3,-5,1,1,0,\ldots,0)\), where first four dates are \(1\)–\(4\). Original outcome \(TSS=100\). Derive the equal-slope normal-equation argument, calculate slope, \(SSR\), detrended \(R^2\), usual full-model \(R^2\) and full-model residual degrees of freedom. Explain what omitted \(\gamma t\) does if \(x\) trends, distinguish level/log/quadratic trend interpretation using a level \(\text{slope}=2\) means \(2\) outcome units per period, and state zero-denominator/rank boundaries. Do these transformations ensure causality or remove all persistent processes? Which \(R^2\) enters a conventional restricted/full-model \(F\) calculation?

Steps and interpretation: Residualised variables are orthogonal to the same intercept/time. Full-model residual \(e\) is orthogonal to \(x,1,t\); substituting \(x_t=a_x+b_xt+\tilde x_t\) gives \(\sum_t\tilde x_t e_t=0\), so \(\widehat\beta=\sum_t\tilde x_t\tilde y_t/\sum_t\tilde x_t^2 = 8/4=2\). Residual \(e=(1,-3,3,-1,0,\ldots), SSR=20\); \(\tilde y\) \(\text{SS}=36\). Detrended \(R^2=1-20/36=0.444444\); full \(R^2=1-20/100=0.800000\); full \(\mathrm{df}=8-3=5\), not a naive residual-stage \(T-2\). The detrended denominator measures variation left after trend, unlike original \(TSS\); use usual consistent restricted/full \(R^2\) for classical \(F\), not this changed denominator. Omitting \(\gamma t\) puts it in \(u\) and may correlate it with trending \(x\), violating zero conditional mean; raw \(R^2\) cannot isolate \(x\). Level trend slope is units/period; log trend for positive \(y\) has approximately \(100\times\text{coefficient}\%\) growth per period; quadratic permits curvature. Declared trend comparison: a level \(\text{slope}=2\) means \(2\) outcome units per period. Residual \(x\) denominator \(0\) means exact collinearity with trend/intercept, no separate slope; residual \(y\) denominator \(0\) makes detrended \(R^2\) undefined. Same controls and rows for every variable are necessary for equal slopes. This is OLS sample algebra and a remedy for the represented deterministic component, not proof of exogeneity/causality or a universal fix for persistence.

sections.html:
Self-assessment criteria and tutor checks

Pass requires every listed component, all requested outputs and essential keyed reasoning without a critical conceptual error. Algebraically equivalent formulas, explicitly defined opposite cash-flow signs and equivalent plain-language reasoning are accepted. Partial means a missing component or a correct method with an unresolved isolated arithmetic slip; fail means the central mechanism or condition is wrong. Unscorable means the response or help/exposure conditions cannot be established. Unknown conditions never certify independence. Arithmetic slips require independent correction before a pass. No numerical grade is invented.

Critical errors: Detrending only \(y\) or using different rows/forms; treating residual regression \(T-2\) \(\mathrm{df}\) as full-model \(\mathrm{df}\); substituting detrended \(R^2\) into classical \(F\); trend removal proves causality.

Acquisition requires two distinct unassisted passes from I1/I2/D1/D2 using the exact six routes in metadata. Each full prompt and key covers every component; any pair therefore covers the whole outcome twice. A fresh D item used for acquisition cannot later certify delayed retention. Worked/support/prerequisite items and the narrow C1 correction cannot substitute for a full check. The finite bank must not be reused after exposure; request a plan_issue when fewer than two fresh full items remain.

sections.html: Seasonality repeats by calendar position, while trend describes movement across dates. For \(m\) positions an intercept plus \(m-1\) indicators uses one omitted reference; each coefficient is an additive difference from that reference at held-fixed substantive regressors. Keeping all \(m\) indicators and intercept causes exact collinearity because their sum equals \(1\). With one \(x\), coefficient count is \(m+1\), plus an extra coefficient if a linear trend is included. Stable seasonal intercept differences are an assumption, not a discovery from adding dummy columns. Partialling out extends the same normal-equation identity: residualise \(y\) and every substantive \(x\) on a joint, identical intercept/calendar/trend basis and same rows, then regress residuals. Full-model degrees of freedom and inferential assumptions survive this computation; naive second-stage outputs need bookkeeping. Regression-based seasonal adjustment is not proof that the data are already adjusted or equivalent to every agency algorithm. Appropriate controls do not themselves establish causal exogeneity or remove serial correlation.
sections.title: Motivation and explanation

sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Seasonality is a repeating calendar pattern; fingerprint 0e7fb5c1af7cabc4ea80572915d3578a657db087254f5d6e70a4f870eabc185f. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Seasonality is a repeating calendar pattern

Monthly or quarterly data may have regular within-year differences. The source's example is retail sales tending to jump in the fourth quarter. Such a pattern differs from a trend: a trend describes systematic movement over time, whereas seasonality repeats with calendar position. It may be represented by seasonal dummy variables or removed before substantive regression by seasonal adjustment. Lecture 2, PDF p. 30

Agent expansion of the seasonal-dummy method: for quarterly data, include an intercept and three indicators, taking quarter 1 as reference:

\[y_t=\beta_0+\beta_1x_t+\lambda_2Q_{2t} +\lambda_3Q_{3t}+\lambda_4Q_{4t}+u_t.\]

Here \(Q_{jt}=1\) if date \(t\) lies in quarter \(j\), otherwise zero. Coefficient \(\lambda_4\) is the fourth-quarter intercept difference relative to quarter 1, holding \(x_t\) fixed. Including all four indicators alongside an intercept would make the intercept their exact sum and violate TS3. Likewise, a model with monthly indicators and an intercept uses eleven independent indicators and one reference month. These designs assume stable additive seasonal differences; writing them does not prove that this is the appropriate adjustment for every dataset. Lecture 2, PDF p. 30; TS3, PDF p. 12

The textbook extends the same partialling-out logic to seasonality: regress the outcome and every substantive regressor on the same intercept and seasonal indicators, then regress their residuals on each other. Their slopes agree with the model that includes those seasonal indicators. A series may contain both a trend and seasonal pattern, so the residualization can include both sets of controls together. This is a simple regression-based adjustment, not a claim that it reproduces every statistical agency's seasonal-adjustment procedure. Wooldridge, 5th ed., PDF p. 401 (printed p. 373)

The supplied lecture gives no numerical seasonal regression or seasonal-adjustment algorithm. It introduces the choice between explicit calendar controls and adjustment of the series before regression; it does not authorize inferring that a supplied series has already been adjusted. Lecture 2, PDF p. 30

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage What the adjustments establish; fingerprint 0e7fb5c1af7cabc4ea80572915d3578a657db087254f5d6e70a4f870eabc185f. Heading depth alone is adapted.

What the adjustments establish

Including a trend or consistently detrending variables changes the comparison from a raw association in levels to a relationship conditional on the chosen time pattern. Seasonal indicators similarly separate stable calendar differences. These are specification tools whose usefulness depends on the relevant time pattern being represented appropriately. They do not by themselves establish causal identification, strict exogeneity, or no serial correlation. The source's unprovided board examples remain unavailable; the algebra here is explicitly agent-created explanation of the uploaded methods. Lecture 2, PDF pp. 27–30

Origin: reused complete note introduction before its first subsection, Stationarity, weak dependence and MA(1), fingerprint 6f5ada6d78aec79c0f8d3419b4cd89e9fa50e130af71d6ca9b0958a4c57bb974. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Stationarity, weak dependence and MA(1)

How can more time observations reveal a stable relationship when they are not independent draws? Week 3 replaces random sampling with conditions that make observations sufficiently informative despite dependence. Stationarity concerns stability of distributions over dates; weak dependence concerns how dependence fades as dates separate. They answer different questions and neither should be inferred simply from a smooth-looking time plot. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 3, 6–13

This map comes from physical pp.7–14; it traces the foundations required for the OLS asymptotic results on pp.20–24. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 7–14, 20–24

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage A process and one observed realization; fingerprint 6f5ada6d78aec79c0f8d3419b4cd89e9fa50e130af71d6ca9b0958a4c57bb974. Heading depth alone is adapted.

A process and one observed realization

A stochastic process \(\{x_t\}\) is a collection of random variables indexed by time. The observed series is one realization of that process, rather than many repetitions at each date. To learn a relationship from a single stretch of history, the mechanism cannot change arbitrarily whenever the observation period changes. Stationarity supplies a particular form of stability; it does not say every realized observation is equal. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 7–8 Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, 5th ed., printed p. 381 (PDF p. 409)

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Strict and covariance stationarity; fingerprint 6f5ada6d78aec79c0f8d3419b4cd89e9fa50e130af71d6ca9b0958a4c57bb974. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Strict and covariance stationarity

The lecture's term stationary means strict stationarity: for every finite set \(t_1<\cdots<t_m\) and permissible shift \(h\), the joint distribution of \((x_{t_1},\ldots,x_{t_m})\) equals that of \((x_{t_1+h},\ldots,x_{t_m+h})\). Single-date distributions are therefore unchanged, and so are joint relationships at fixed lags. The definition allows strong adjacent correlation; what cannot change is the distributional pattern when all dates shift together. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 8

If second moments exist, covariance stationarity requires only

\[E[x_t]=\mu,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(x_t)=\gamma(0),\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(x_t,x_{t+h})=\gamma(h),\]

where \(\mu,\gamma(0)\) are finite constants and \(\gamma(h)\) depends on lag \(h\), not calendar date \(t\). Strict stationarity with finite second moments implies these moment restrictions; the converse need not hold because higher-order distributional features may change. The opening sentence on lecture p.10 calls covariance stationarity a “special case,” but its later finite-moment implication correctly identifies it as a weaker condition. An observed sample mean/variance is a diagnostic, not proof of an unchanged population distribution. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 10 Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, 5th ed., printed p. 381 (PDF p. 409) Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, 5th ed., printed p. 382 (PDF p. 410)

Physical p.9 compares different time windows (roughly100–300 and600–800). The left series has similar location/spread and overlapping histograms; the right shifts in location. This illustrates distributional stability rather than constituting a statistical test. The second right-hand histogram legend mistakenly uses an \(x\) label despite the plotted right series being \(y\); do not infer a third variable. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 9

Weak dependence and why limit theorems need it

Weak dependence means that sufficiently distant observations are nearly independent in the sense required by the relevant limit theorem. The lecture uses a covariance-stationary intuition: \(\operatorname{Corr}(x_t,x_{t+h})\to0\) sufficiently rapidly as \(h\to\infty\). That rate qualification matters. Pairwise zero or vanishing correlation alone is not a universal independence condition or a complete general CLT assumption. The lecture deliberately leaves formal definitions outside scope. Its stationarity-based introduction on p.12 is a convenient setting, not a universal rule that a process with deterministic trend can never have weakly dependent deviations; p.18 and the textbook explicitly allow that distinction. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 12–13, 18 Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, 5th ed., printed p. 382 (PDF p. 410)

The law of large numbers (LLN) makes suitable sample averages approach their population counterparts. The central limit theorem (CLT) describes the scaled fluctuation around those limits and supports approximate normal inference. With independent draws these results are familiar; for time series they need dependence and moment regularity strong enough for the required averages. More observations of an almost permanently shared shock need not act like more independent information. This is why weak dependence is a substantive prerequisite, not a cosmetic relabeling of random sampling. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 6–7, 12–13, 20

sections.title: Content provenance and generation boundaries

sections.html:
Read the full checked source context

How can more time observations reveal a stable relationship when they are not independent draws? Week 3 replaces random sampling with conditions that make observations sufficiently informative despite dependence. Stationarity concerns stability of distributions over dates; weak dependence concerns how dependence fades as dates separate. They answer different questions and neither should be inferred simply from a smooth-looking time plot. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 3, 6–13

This map comes from physical pp.7–14; it traces the foundations required for the OLS asymptotic results on pp.20–24. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 7–14, 20–24

A process and one observed realization

A stochastic process \(\{x_t\}\) is a collection of random variables indexed by time. The observed series is one realization of that process, rather than many repetitions at each date. To learn a relationship from a single stretch of history, the mechanism cannot change arbitrarily whenever the observation period changes. Stationarity supplies a particular form of stability; it does not say every realized observation is equal. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 7–8 Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, 5th ed., printed p. 381 (PDF p. 409)

Strict and covariance stationarity

The lecture's term stationary means strict stationarity: for every finite set \(t_1<\cdots<t_m\) and permissible shift \(h\), the joint distribution of \((x_{t_1},\ldots,x_{t_m})\) equals that of \((x_{t_1+h},\ldots,x_{t_m+h})\). Single-date distributions are therefore unchanged, and so are joint relationships at fixed lags. The definition allows strong adjacent correlation; what cannot change is the distributional pattern when all dates shift together. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 8

If second moments exist, covariance stationarity requires only

\[E[x_t]=\mu,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(x_t)=\gamma(0),\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(x_t,x_{t+h})=\gamma(h),\]

where \(\mu,\gamma(0)\) are finite constants and \(\gamma(h)\) depends on lag \(h\), not calendar date \(t\). Strict stationarity with finite second moments implies these moment restrictions; the converse need not hold because higher-order distributional features may change. The opening sentence on lecture p.10 calls covariance stationarity a “special case,” but its later finite-moment implication correctly identifies it as a weaker condition. An observed sample mean/variance is a diagnostic, not proof of an unchanged population distribution. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 10 Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, 5th ed., printed p. 381 (PDF p. 409) Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, 5th ed., printed p. 382 (PDF p. 410)

Physical p.9 compares different time windows (roughly100–300 and600–800). The left series has similar location/spread and overlapping histograms; the right shifts in location. This illustrates distributional stability rather than constituting a statistical test. The second right-hand histogram legend mistakenly uses an \(x\) label despite the plotted right series being \(y\); do not infer a third variable. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 9

The restaurant-price index on the appended physical p.32 changes its level over the sample; p.11 classifies it as nonstationary. A deterministic trend also changes the mean. The plot alone does not tell whether detrending or differencing is the correct remedy, because deterministic and stochastic trends are different mechanisms. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 11, 18, 30, 32

Weak dependence and why limit theorems need it

Weak dependence means that sufficiently distant observations are nearly independent in the sense required by the relevant limit theorem. The lecture uses a covariance-stationary intuition: \(\operatorname{Corr}(x_t,x_{t+h})\to0\) sufficiently rapidly as \(h\to\infty\). That rate qualification matters. Pairwise zero or vanishing correlation alone is not a universal independence condition or a complete general CLT assumption. The lecture deliberately leaves formal definitions outside scope. Its stationarity-based introduction on p.12 is a convenient setting, not a universal rule that a process with deterministic trend can never have weakly dependent deviations; p.18 and the textbook explicitly allow that distinction. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 12–13, 18 Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, 5th ed., printed p. 382 (PDF p. 410)

The law of large numbers (LLN) makes suitable sample averages approach their population counterparts. The central limit theorem (CLT) describes the scaled fluctuation around those limits and supports approximate normal inference. With independent draws these results are familiar; for time series they need dependence and moment regularity strong enough for the required averages. More observations of an almost permanently shared shock need not act like more independent information. This is why weak dependence is a substantive prerequisite, not a cosmetic relabeling of random sampling. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 6–7, 12–13, 20

MA(1): dependence with a finite reach

Let

\[x_t=\varepsilon_t+\alpha\varepsilon_{t-1},\]

where innovations \(\varepsilon_t\) are i.i.d., have mean zero and finite positive variance \(\sigma_\varepsilon^2\). This is a data-generating process, not necessarily a regression equation. The same fixed transformation of identically distributed innovation blocks at every date gives strict stationarity. Independence eliminates cross terms, so

\[E[x_t]=0,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(x_t)=(1+\alpha^2)\sigma_\varepsilon^2.\]

Adjacent values share \(\varepsilon_t\):

\[\operatorname{Cov}(x_t,x_{t+1})=\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_t+\alpha\varepsilon_{t-1},\varepsilon_{t+1}+\alpha\varepsilon_t)=\alpha\sigma_\varepsilon^2,\]

\[\operatorname{Corr}(x_t,x_{t+1})=\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha^2}.\]

At lag two or more, the innovation sets are disjoint, hence the values are independent under the stated i.i.d. assumption. Dependence ends after one lag; it need not be zero at lag one for the process to be weakly dependent. No \(|\alpha|<1\) restriction is needed for this stationarity argument; a different invertibility question is not part of this lecture. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 11, 14 Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, 5th ed., printed p. 383 (PDF p. 411)

Reading priority and prerequisites

Strict-versus-moment stability and weak dependence are core foundations because they justify the assumptions used by the later consistency/inference theorems. Covariance algebra and independent innovations are prerequisites for understanding why MA(1) dependence ends and AR(1) dependence fades; memorizing the labels does not supply that reasoning. The histogram/restaurant examples support diagnosis but cannot replace those definitions. Continue with the AR(1)/random-walk note, then the OLS asymptotic note. This is a conceptual reading path, not an assessment prediction. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 7–17, 20–30

O015-W1, item_version 1, worked_example. Prompt: Let \(x_t=\varepsilon_t+\alpha\varepsilon_{t-1}\) for an i.i.d. innovation sequence defined at all required integer dates, \(E[\varepsilon_t]=0\), \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_t)=4>0\), and \(\alpha=0.5\). sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
Origin: reused complete note introduction before its first subsection, AR(1), random walks and integration, fingerprint 710163a54be6e9043b101fb7c24a6ba169ce5ba3899e3cd065fab4a095829965. Heading depth alone is adapted.

AR(1), random walks and integration

Does a shock fade away, or does it permanently change the level of a series? Comparing a stable autoregression with a random walk explains why apparent persistence changes the validity of ordinary regression asymptotics. It also separates removing a deterministic trend from differencing an accumulated random shock. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 15–18, 25–30

The diagram follows physical pp.15–18 and26–30; stationary moments/independent innovations are explained in the preceding Week3 note. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 15–18, 26–30

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Stable AR(1): assumptions before moments; fingerprint 710163a54be6e9043b101fb7c24a6ba169ce5ba3899e3cd065fab4a095829965. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Stable AR(1): assumptions before moments

An autoregression of order one obeys

\[x_t=\rho x_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t,\]

with i.i.d. zero-mean innovations of finite variance \(\sigma_\varepsilon^2>0\). Future innovations must be independent of the initial value/past. The stability condition is \(|\rho|<1\). To derive the lecture's constant moments from the start, take a covariance-stationary initialization; the recurrence and stability alone do not guarantee that an arbitrary fixed or random \(x_0\) has the stationary distribution. The lecture omits that initialization qualification on p.15; the textbook explicitly assumes covariance stationarity in the displayed moment argument. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 15–16 Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, 5th ed., printed p. 383 (PDF p. 411)

Under stationary initialization, the mean satisfies \(\mu=\rho\mu\), giving \(\mu=0\) because \(\rho\ne1\). Independence of the innovation from the past gives

\[\sigma_x^2=\rho^2\sigma_x^2+\sigma_\varepsilon^2,\qquad \sigma_x^2=\frac{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}{1-\rho^2}.\]

The positive denominator is why a nondegenerate finite stationary variance is compatible with \(|\rho|<1\). A recurrence started instead at fixed zero has

\[\operatorname{Var}(x_t)=\sigma_\varepsilon^2\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}\rho^{2j}=\sigma_\varepsilon^2\frac{1-\rho^{2t}}{1-\rho^2},\]

which approaches the stationary variance but is not equal to it at every finite date. This last expression is agent-derived qualification: repeatedly substitute the recurrence, then add variances of independent shocks. It shows exactly what the missing initialization changes. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 15–16 Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, 5th ed., printed p. 383 (PDF p. 411)

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Why AR(1) correlation fades; fingerprint 710163a54be6e9043b101fb7c24a6ba169ce5ba3899e3cd065fab4a095829965. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Why AR(1) correlation fades

Substitution over \(h\) future periods gives

\[x_{t+h}=\rho^h x_t+\sum_{j=1}^{h}\rho^{h-j}\varepsilon_{t+j}.\]

Future innovations have zero covariance with \(x_t\), so under the stationary moments

\[\operatorname{Cov}(x_t,x_{t+h})=\rho^h\sigma_x^2,\qquad \operatorname{Corr}(x_t,x_{t+h})=\rho^h.\]

Thus correlation tends to zero geometrically when \(|\rho|<1\). Negative \(\rho\) alternates the sign; a \(\rho\) near one decays slowly in a short sample but remains stable. Under zero conditional-mean future innovations, \(E[x_{t+h}\mid x_t]=\rho^h x_t\) approaches zero. This is the mechanism behind fading shocks, rather than a claim that adjacent values are independent. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 17, 27 Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, 5th ed., printed p. 384 (PDF p. 412)

sections.html:
O016-W1, item_version 1, worked_example. Prompt: For \(x_t=\rho x_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t\), take \(\rho=0.5\), i.i.d. zero-mean innovations of variance 3, independent of the initial value/past. Under covariance-stationary initialization derive mean, variance, lag-2 covariance/correlation and forecast from current \(x_t=8\). Compare with initialization \(x_0=0\) by computing variance at date 2. Explain stability, shock decay and the distinction between a near-unit-root stable coefficient and an exact random walk. Does the recurrence with \(|\rho|<1\) alone force stationary finite-date moments from an arbitrary initialization?

Complete solution and essential rubric: With \(|\rho|<1\) and stationary initialization, \(\mu=\rho\mu\) implies \(\mu=0\). Independence gives \(\sigma_x^2=\rho^2\sigma_x^2+\sigma_\varepsilon^2\), hence \(\sigma_x^2=4.00000000\). Iteration gives \(x_{t+h}=\rho^h x_t+\sum_{j=1}^h\rho^{h-j}\varepsilon_{t+j}\). Future innovations have zero covariance/conditional mean given the past, so lag \(2\) covariance is \(\rho^2\sigma_x^2=1.00000000\), correlation \(\rho^2=0.25000000\) and conditional forecast \(\rho^2(8)=2.00000000\). With fixed zero initialization, variance at date \(2\) is \(\sigma_\varepsilon^2(1-\rho^{2t})/(1-\rho^2)=3.75000000\); it approaches but generally is not the stationary variance at a finite date. Thus stability/recurrence alone does not supply stationary initialization. Powers decay to zero; negative \(\rho\) alternates signs and a value near one decays slowly without equaling a unit root. At \(\rho\) one shocks accumulate instead. Constant population moments and sample appearances are distinct. sections.title: Content provenance and generation boundaries

sections.html:
Read the full checked source context

Does a shock fade away, or does it permanently change the level of a series? Comparing a stable autoregression with a random walk explains why apparent persistence changes the validity of ordinary regression asymptotics. It also separates removing a deterministic trend from differencing an accumulated random shock. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 15–18, 25–30

The diagram follows physical pp.15–18 and26–30; stationary moments/independent innovations are explained in the preceding Week3 note. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 15–18, 26–30

Stable AR(1): assumptions before moments

An autoregression of order one obeys

\[x_t=\rho x_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t,\]

with i.i.d. zero-mean innovations of finite variance \(\sigma_\varepsilon^2>0\). Future innovations must be independent of the initial value/past. The stability condition is \(|\rho|<1\). To derive the lecture's constant moments from the start, take a covariance-stationary initialization; the recurrence and stability alone do not guarantee that an arbitrary fixed or random \(x_0\) has the stationary distribution. The lecture omits that initialization qualification on p.15; the textbook explicitly assumes covariance stationarity in the displayed moment argument. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 15–16 Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, 5th ed., printed p. 383 (PDF p. 411)

Under stationary initialization, the mean satisfies \(\mu=\rho\mu\), giving \(\mu=0\) because \(\rho\ne1\). Independence of the innovation from the past gives

\[\sigma_x^2=\rho^2\sigma_x^2+\sigma_\varepsilon^2,\qquad \sigma_x^2=\frac{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}{1-\rho^2}.\]

The positive denominator is why a nondegenerate finite stationary variance is compatible with \(|\rho|<1\). A recurrence started instead at fixed zero has

\[\operatorname{Var}(x_t)=\sigma_\varepsilon^2\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}\rho^{2j}=\sigma_\varepsilon^2\frac{1-\rho^{2t}}{1-\rho^2},\]

which approaches the stationary variance but is not equal to it at every finite date. This last expression is agent-derived qualification: repeatedly substitute the recurrence, then add variances of independent shocks. It shows exactly what the missing initialization changes. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 15–16 Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, 5th ed., printed p. 383 (PDF p. 411)

Why AR(1) correlation fades

Substitution over \(h\) future periods gives

\[x_{t+h}=\rho^h x_t+\sum_{j=1}^{h}\rho^{h-j}\varepsilon_{t+j}.\]

Future innovations have zero covariance with \(x_t\), so under the stationary moments

\[\operatorname{Cov}(x_t,x_{t+h})=\rho^h\sigma_x^2,\qquad \operatorname{Corr}(x_t,x_{t+h})=\rho^h.\]

Thus correlation tends to zero geometrically when \(|\rho|<1\). Negative \(\rho\) alternates the sign; a \(\rho\) near one decays slowly in a short sample but remains stable. Under zero conditional-mean future innovations, \(E[x_{t+h}\mid x_t]=\rho^h x_t\) approaches zero. This is the mechanism behind fading shocks, rather than a claim that adjacent values are independent. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 17, 27 Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, 5th ed., printed p. 384 (PDF p. 412)

Random walk: constant mean does not imply stationarity

Set \(\rho=1\). Repeated substitution gives

\[x_t=x_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t=x_0+\sum_{j=1}^{t}\varepsilon_j.\]

For \(x_0\) independent of the innovations,

\[E[x_t]=E[x_0],\qquad \operatorname{Var}(x_t)=\operatorname{Var}(x_0)+t\sigma_\varepsilon^2.\]

If \(x_0=c\) is fixed, these become \(E[x_t]=c\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(x_t)=t\sigma_\varepsilon^2\). Increasing variance prevents covariance stationarity even with a constant mean. Source qualification: p.26 first allows an independent initial value but then writes \(E[x_0]=x_0\) and drops \(\operatorname{Var}(x_0)\). Those reductions require fixed \(x_0\); for random \(x_0\) retain its expectation and variance. The textbook distinguishes the cases explicitly. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 26 Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, 5th ed., printed p. 392 (PDF p. 420)

Conditional prediction is

\[E[x_{t+h}\mid x_t]=x_t.\]

A shock to today's level enters every future level with coefficient one. This contrasts with \(\rho^h\) for stable AR(1), and explains permanent versus fading shocks. A random walk is one example of a unit-root process. A high sample lag-one correlation is suggestive of persistence, but it does not itself prove an exact unit root. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 27, 30

Drift and deterministic trend are different

For a random walk with drift \(a\),

\[x_t=a+x_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t=x_0+at+\sum_{j=1}^{t}\varepsilon_j,\]

\[E[x_t]=E[x_0]+at,\quad \operatorname{Var}(x_t)=\operatorname{Var}(x_0)+t\sigma_\varepsilon^2,\quad E[x_{t+h}\mid x_t]=x_t+ah.\]

The deterministic mean trend \(at\) does not remove accumulated random shocks. Subtracting \(at\) leaves a random walk. By contrast, a trend-stationary process \(z_t=b_0+b_1t+v_t\) has stationary weakly dependent deviations \(v_t\); removing the correct deterministic trend exposes those deviations. The lecture's “include a trend” reassurance on p.18 concerns that case and still requires valid regression assumptions. It is not a remedy for any series that rises over time. Persistence can exist without a visible trend (the lecture names interest rates, inflation and unemployment), and a trend can exist without persistent stochastic shocks. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 18, 28, 30 Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, 5th ed., printed p. 394 (PDF p. 422) Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, 5th ed., printed p. 395 (PDF p. 423)

Integration and first differences

In this course's framing, an \(I(0)\) process has the weak-dependence properties needed for ordinary limit-theorem reasoning; an \(I(1)\) level requires one difference to obtain such a process. For the random walk,

\[\Delta x_t=x_t-x_{t-1}=\varepsilon_t,\]

so differences are i.i.d. and \(I(0)\) even though levels are \(I(1)\). With drift the difference is \(a+\varepsilon_t\). General \(I(1)\) differences need not be i.i.d.; they may retain weak serial dependence. Differencing changes the modeled variable from its level to its period-to-period change, so coefficients must be interpreted accordingly. It does not automatically cure endogeneity or every inference problem. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 29 Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, 5th ed., printed p. 396 (PDF p. 424)

For a deterministic trend, \(\Delta z_t=b_1+\Delta v_t\), which also removes its changing mean but may alter short-run dependence. Choosing between detrending and differencing therefore requires a process argument; “both remove a visible trend” is insufficient. Online verification: Hyndman and Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice, 3rd ed., §9.1 “Stationarity and differencing,” subsections “Differencing” and “Random walk model,” confirms the random-walk transformation and warns that unnecessary differencing can introduce autocorrelation. Consulted author textbook section. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 18, 29–30

What the lecture does and does not test

Physical p.30 advises looking at lag-one correlation and names Dickey–Fuller and augmented Dickey–Fuller tests, referring to textbook Chapter18.2. The supplied slides do not provide those tests' regressions, null distributions, critical values or worked applications, so naming them is not a prepared test procedure. The instruction “Detrend first!” is supported here only as a warning that a deterministic trend can inflate estimated autocorrelation; it does not mean detrending makes every unit-root series stationary. Wooldridge, 5th ed., printed p.398 (PDF p.426) Formal unit-root-testing instruction beyond the source's pointers remains outside this note. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 30 Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, 5th ed., printed p. 397 (PDF p. 425)

Spurious regression is the danger that unrelated persistent series in levels display a misleading apparent relationship, potentially accompanied by large fit or seemingly significant usual test statistics. Shared-looking movements in one observed history need not represent an economic connection. If an accumulated random shock is mistaken for a deterministic trend, removing a fitted line still leaves the stochastic persistence; the weak-dependence conditions justifying the ordinary inference above have not thereby been restored. This is the warning on lecture p.30, rather than a claim that every regression containing an \(I(1)\) variable is necessarily spurious. The lecture postpones formal analysis. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p.30 Wooldridge, 5th ed., printed p.395 (PDF p.423)

The source's restaurant index shows variation and a later level change. Together with the simulated comparison on p.9 it motivates checking stability, but supplies no fitted DGP or formal test result. The red vertical marker has no explained causal interpretation in the supplied page; none is assigned here. 2026_Lecture3_print.pdf, physical PDF p. 11, 32
